["question-6e09043a-2656-5006-b96f-e232ecdf95b0" :question/math-academy-id "q-344045"] ["question-6e09043a-2656-5006-b96f-e232ecdf95b0" :question/problem "$$
{y}^{″}+5{\pi }^{2}y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0
$$

Consider the initial value problem above, where $f(x)$ is an odd, $4$-periodic function. Select the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the second infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution of the differential equation.

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{20(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{3}(20-{n}^{2})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})
$$"] ["question-6e09043a-2656-5006-b96f-e232ecdf95b0" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(x)$ is given by $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},$ where ${y}_{c}$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we address the particular solution ${y}_{p}.$ Since $f(x)$ is an odd function, its Fourier series consists only of sine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function. This is represented by the term

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{20(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{3}(20-{n}^{2})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Next, we find the homogeneous solution. The characteristic equation ${\lambda }^{2}+5{\pi }^{2}=0$ gives roots $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{5}\pi \,\text{i}.$ So, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}\pi x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Using $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+0+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ because the particular solution is a sine series.

Next, we use the derivative condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0.$ First, we compute the derivative of the total solution (with $A=0$):

$$
{y}^{′}(x)∼B\sqrt{5}\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}\pi x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{10(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(20-{n}^{2})}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})
$$

Applying ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ and noting that $\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =B\sqrt{5}\pi +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{10(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(20-{n}^{2})} \\ B\sqrt{5}\pi  & =-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{10(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(20-{n}^{2})} \\ B & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{10(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(20-{n}^{2})} \\  & =-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{10(-1)^{n}}{n\sqrt{5}{\pi }^{3}(20-{n}^{2})} \\  & =-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2\sqrt{5}(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{3}(20-{n}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $B$ back into ${y}_{c}=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}\pi x)$, we find the missing part:

$$
y(x)∼-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}\pi x){\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2\sqrt{5}(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{3}(20-{n}^{2})}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{20(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{3}(20-{n}^{2})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})
$$"] ["question-6e09043a-2656-5006-b96f-e232ecdf95b0" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-ca20e363-d96f-5c7c-870a-e0d6761fc82a" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-1f6be087-1fa7-52c8-8b37-3dc253f9f151" :question/problem "If $\frac{2y}{6y+1}+Z=\frac{x+1}{3x},$ then what is $Z?$"] ["question-1f6be087-1fa7-52c8-8b37-3dc253f9f151" :question/worked-solution "Since $\frac{2y}{6y+1}+Z=\frac{x+1}{3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Z & =\frac{x+1}{3x}-\frac{2y}{6y+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to put the fractions over a common denominator of $3x(6y+1),$ since there are no common factors in either denominator that we can exploit. 

To do this, we multiply the top and bottom of the first fraction by $6y+1,$ and the top and bottom of the second fraction by $3x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}Z & =\frac{x+1}{3x}-\frac{2y}{6y+1} \\  & =\frac{6y+1}{6y+1}\cdot \frac{x+1}{3x}-\frac{3x}{3x}\cdot \frac{2y}{6y+1} \\  & =\frac{(6y+1)(x+1)}{3x(6y+1)}-\frac{3x(2y)}{3x(6y+1)} \\  & =\frac{(6y+1)(x+1)-3x(2y)}{3x(6y+1)} \\  & =\frac{6yx+x+6y+1-6xy}{3x(6y+1)} \\  & =\frac{x+6y+1}{3x(6y+1)}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-1f6be087-1fa7-52c8-8b37-3dc253f9f151" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-76acf816-9d43-55de-b720-1823543ac3f0" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}-\frac{(z-1)^{2}}{5} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}-1 & =\frac{(z-1)^{2}}{5} \\ (z-1)^{2} & =5(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}-1) \\ (z-1) & =\pm \sqrt{5(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}-1)}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the square root is defined only for non-negative arguments, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}-1 & \ge 0 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8} & \ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the exterior of the ellipse $\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}=1$, including its boundary.

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}\ge 1\}.
$$"] ["answer-bea4c84f-b068-5e60-82b9-448a2bf9137c" :answer/id #uuid "bea4c84f-b068-5e60-82b9-448a2bf9137c"] ["answer-bea4c84f-b068-5e60-82b9-448a2bf9137c" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["question-30e8d5c3-bff2-59db-90d6-3878e212499e" :question/math-academy-id "q-71962"] ["question-30e8d5c3-bff2-59db-90d6-3878e212499e" :question/problem "The projection of the intersection between the hyperboloid of two sheets $\frac{5(x-1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{5(y-2)^{2}}{16}+\frac{(z-3)^{2}}{4}=-1$ and the plane $z=2$ onto the $xy$-plane is a hyperbola. What are the lengths of the semi-axes of the hyperbola?"] ["question-30e8d5c3-bff2-59db-90d6-3878e212499e" :question/worked-solution "To find the intersection of the hyperboloid and the plane $z=2$, we substitute $z=2$ into the equation of the hyperboloid:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5(x-1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{5(y-2)^{2}}{16}+\frac{(2-3)^{2}}{4} & =-1 \\ \frac{5(x-1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{5(y-2)^{2}}{16}+\frac{1}{4} & =-1 \\ \frac{5(x-1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{5(y-2)^{2}}{16} & =-1-\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{5(x-1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{5(y-2)^{2}}{16} & =-\frac{5}{4} \\ -(x-1)^{2}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ -\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a hyperbola with semi-axes of lengths $1$ and $2.$"] ["question-30e8d5c3-bff2-59db-90d6-3878e212499e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] $$

$$

$$
{P}^{′}=kP(a-P),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.

For a logistic growth model, the fastest rate of growth occurs when $P=\frac{1}{2}a.$

![](images/9d/9d8f5340bba4d3c407e43f2bc64a4aa2ea986be89b8024baaa4e8ae65e96e5d5.png)

First, let's rewrite the right-hand side of the given equation so that it matches the form above:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{dt} & =12P-0.000\,2{P}^{2} \\  & =0.000\,02P(60\,000-P)\end{aligned}
$$

From here, we see that $a=60\,000.$ Hence, the carrying capacity is $60\,000,$ and $P$ grows at its fastest possible rate when 

$$
P=\frac{1}{2}a=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 60\,000=30\,000.
$$"] ["question-b63e7390-032d-5732-93f4-683f3a627416" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-c19ec431-2d31-55ac-9370-03580e2d85ee" :answer-field/id #uuid {{field-1}}"] ["question-b8a8e489-11e9-52ae-86cf-436bdb177f60" :question/worked-solution "A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
{P}^{′}=kP(a-P),

For a logistic growth model, the fastest rate of growth occurs when $P=\frac{1}{2}a.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{dt} & =5P-0.001{P}^{2} \\  & =0.001P(5000-P)\end{aligned}
$$

From here, we see that $a=5000.$ Hence, the carrying capacity is $5000,$ and $P$ grows at its fastest possible rate when 

$$
P=\frac{1}{2}a=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 5000=2500.
$$"] ["question-b8a8e489-11e9-52ae-86cf-436bdb177f60" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-aa8b8268-0d26-5cf4-8d60-0789f0a8afa9" :answer-field/id #uuid Therefore, the correct answer is "$\mathcal{P}$ only.""] [17592186073600 :question/worked-solution "First, let's find the measures of unknown angles. Since the sum of the measures of internal angles of a quadrilateral is $360^\circ$, we have

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""] [17592186074983 :tutorial/content "Two polygons are **similar** if they have the same shape (though they may have different sizes).

More precisely, two polygons are similar if the following conditions hold:

1. Their corresponding angles are congruent.
2. The ratios of the lengths of their corresponding sides are all equal.

To demonstrate, let's consider the triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle EFG$ below.

![](images/23/233fcb591a81d9ee6eef3caf1f4df0f0e959a18144177e89d5f0ac88c94525f4.png)

From the figure above, we see that the corresponding angles are congruent:

$$
\angle A \cong \angle E, \qquad \angle B \cong \angle F, \qquad \angle C \cong \angle G
$$

We also need to check whether the ratios of the corresponding sides are the same. That is, we have to check whether

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{AB}{EF} &= \frac{BC}{FG} = \frac{AC}{EG}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the lengths of the sides, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{AB}{EF} &= \frac{6}{12} = \frac{1}{2} \\
\frac{BC}{FG} &= \frac{4}{8} = \frac{1}{2} \\
\frac{AC}{EG} &= \frac{5}{10} = \frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

The ratios are the same. Therefore, we conclude that the triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle EFG$ are similar. The common ratio of the sides,

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

is called the **similarity ratio**.

To express mathematically that the triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle EFG$ are similar, we write

$$
\triangle ABC \sim \triangle EFG
$$"] [17592186075009 :tutorial/content "When writing a similarity statement, corresponding vertices should appear in the same position in the statement. For example, if we're given that

To figure out what we need to multiply by, we can set up an equation to help us:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{mg}}{\textrm{m}}\cdot\, \dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{m}}
$$

We want to replace $\textrm{mg}$ with $\textrm{g}$. To get rid of $\textrm{mg}$, we can put $\textrm{mg}$ in the denominator so that it cancels out. To introduce $\textrm{g}$, we can put $\textrm{g}$ in the numerator.

$$
\require{cancel} \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{mg}}}{\textrm{m}}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\cancel{\textrm{mg}}} = \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{m}}
$$

So, our conversion formula is

$$
\require{cancel} \dfrac{\textrm{mg}}{\textrm{m}}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{mg}} = \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{m}}
$$

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use, and apply it.

- The density given in the problem statement is $3\,950 \, \dfrac{\textrm{mg}}{\textrm{m}}$.
- There are $1\,000$ milligrams per gram. Taking the reciprocal, there are $\dfrac{1}{1\,000}$ grams per milligram.

Applying our conversion formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
3950\frac{mg}{m} &= 3950\frac{mg}{m} \cdot \frac{1}{1000}\frac{g}{mg} \\
&= (3950 \cdot \frac{1}{1000})\frac{mg}{m} \cdot \frac{g}{mg} \\
&= 3.95\frac{g}{m}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the linear mass density of the string is $3.95\,\textrm{g}/\textrm{m}$."] [17592186138315 :question/worked-solution "We are given the units

17592186385291}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+2y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,y(1)=3
$$

where $f(x)$ is $1$-periodic and odd. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0.$*

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$" :question/worked-solution "We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+2y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0$, we have

$$
y(0)={y}_{c}(0)\,\text{and}\,y(1)={y}_{c}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

- Use $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+B(0)+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).$

- Use $y(1)=3$ with $A=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})+{y}_{p}(1) \\ 3 & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})+0 \\ B & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186231574 :question/id #uuid "0f970b89-f8e7-590f-9e3b-8ad7dbd8f9e1" :question/math-academy-id "q-343669"} {:db/id 17592186372872 :question/id #uuid "356f9e42-beaf-5ba9-bd6f-c8cc225eace9" :question/math-academy-id "q-344318"} {:db/id 17592186372878 :question/id #uuid "9b96aedd-ce80-5f05-9df5-d9873f821b74" :question/math-academy-id "q-344321" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a1ee564-8e0f-5ee0-998f-2101fc9cd57a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)" :db/id 17592186372880} {:answer/id #uuid "0c1903c2-0865-5c88-ad0e-67617d3c44ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3)}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)" :db/id 17592186372881} {:answer/id #uuid "6005d9a8-46b9-5819-acc2-87a742a05929" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2)}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)" :db/id 17592186372882} {:answer/id #uuid "3078353a-b59d-5067-b6f6-a1a830986836" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3)}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)" :db/id 17592186372883}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186372883} :answer-field/id #uuid "01f8df2d-ecbb-512a-aa1b-2ac650da1f39" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186372879}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

17592186231788 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231986 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we will use Fourier series to solve boundary value problems with periodic forcing functions.

As before, we consider a second-order linear differential equation with constant coefficients and forcing function $f(x)$, for which the general solution can be written as

$$
y=y_c+y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

The main ideas are similar to those of solving IVPs:

- we choose the correct form of the series for the particular solution $y_p$, and then

- use boundary conditions at the endpoints to determine the constants in the homogeneous part $y_c$ of the solution.

When $f(x)$ is periodic, we often look for $y_p$ as a Fourier series on a symmetric interval $[-L,L].$

Recall that for an equation of the form $y''+\omega^2 y=f(x)$ with no (damping) $y'$ term, the particular solution inherits the parity of $f(x)$:

- If $f$ is *even*, then its Fourier series contains only cosine terms.

- If $f$ is *odd*, then its Fourier series contains only sine terms.

For example, consider the boundary value problem

$$
y''+5y=f(x)
$$

on $[-2,2]$, where $f$ is $4$-periodic and odd. We want the appropriate Fourier series form for a particular solution $y_p$.

Because $f$ is $4$-periodic on $[-2,2]$, we have $L=2$, so the Fourier basis on this interval is

$$
\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

Next, since $f$ is odd, its Fourier series contains only sine terms. Since the equation has no $y'$ term, the particular solution inherits the same parity and is also odd.

Therefore, the appropriate form for $y_p$ is a sine series:

$$
y_p(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

Let's see more examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "67a0ca11-7450-5f6a-8bdc-4aee6301f209" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14775 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid $$
y=y_c+y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

There are many types of boundary conditions (including mixed or Robin-type conditions), but in this lesson, we will focus on the two simplest cases:

- *Dirichlet conditions* (values of $y$ are specified):

$$
y(a)=\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y(b)=\beta
$$

- *Neumann conditions* (values of $y'$ are specified):

$$
y'(a)=\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(b)=\beta
$$

A key simplification is possible if we choose our particular solution $y_p$ to satisfy the corresponding *homogeneous* boundary conditions. For any given $f(x),$ it is always possible to find such a $y_p$. 
This drastically simplifies the computations, as the boundary conditions then determine the constants in $y_c$ directly.

- *Dirichlet-type simplification:* If we choose the forcing so that

$$
y_p(a)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_p(b)=0,
$$

then

$$
y(a)=y_c(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y(b)=y_c(b),
$$

so we can solve for the constants in $y_c$ using only the homogeneous solution.

- *Neumann-type simplification:* If we choose the forcing so that

$$
y_p'(a)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_p'(b)=0,
$$

then

$$
y'(a)=y_c'(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(b)=y_c'(b),
$$

so the derivative conditions determine the constants in $y_c$ directly.

Let's see how this works in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "16e90dd1-2074-5728-ad7b-e05a00c3e171" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14795 :tutorial/title "Using Boundary Conditions"} :step/id #uuid "46704bc7-b368-569c-9ed3-f228bcfd99b9" :step/math-academy-id 601983 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231790}}] :activity/title "Solving BVPs Using Fourier Series" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186231522} {:db/id 17592186231788 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231986 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we will use Fourier series to solve boundary value problems with periodic forcing functions.

$$
y=y_c+y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

There are many types of boundary conditions (including mixed or Robin-type conditions), but in this lesson, we will focus on the two simplest cases:

- *Dirichlet conditions* (values of $y$ are specified):

$$
y(a)=\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y(b)=\beta
$$

- *Neumann conditions* (values of $y'$ are specified):

$$
y'(a)=\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(b)=\beta
$$

A key simplification is possible if we choose our particular solution $y_p$ to satisfy the corresponding *homogeneous* boundary conditions. For any given $f(x),$ it is always possible to find such a $y_p$. 
This drastically simplifies the computations, as the boundary conditions then determine the constants in $y_c$ directly.

- *Dirichlet-type simplification:* If we choose the forcing so that

$$
y_p(a)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_p(b)=0,
$$

then

$$
y(a)=y_c(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y(b)=y_c(b),
$$

so we can solve for the constants in $y_c$ using only the homogeneous solution.

- *Neumann-type simplification:* If we choose the forcing so that

$$
y_p'(a)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_p'(b)=0,
$$

then

$$
y'(a)=y_c'(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(b)=y_c'(b),
$$

so the derivative conditions determine the constants in $y_c$ directly.

$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Because $f$ is $6$-periodic on $[-3,3]$, we have $L=3$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\,\text{and}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a cosine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3cad45fa-b76b-5d49-807e-179e9cf7aed9" :step/next {:db/id 17592186509037}} {:db/id 17592186509012 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231573 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "71a6be11-8878-5070-81b7-b47676c4ce8d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2})}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)" :db/id 17592186385292} {:answer/id #uuid "5ce9062b-d93f-55c2-a03a-1ae8c327c26f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x)" :db/id 17592186385293} {:answer/id #uuid "9fa04091-bc19-5979-8a5e-2e3897f35181" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2)}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)" :db/id 17592186385294} {:answer/id #uuid "2ee0778f-6531-5ab8-bddf-60696be3a1d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)" :db/id 17592186385295}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186385295} :answer-field/id #uuid "9ecdd4ec-27ca-5ae4-9688-c8b8aa4f79ea" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186385291}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "6a08e9ea-1ab7-5988-bf4e-d55c1dd407e0" :question/math-academy-id "q-343668" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0$, we have

$$
y(0)={y}_{c}(0)\,\text{and}\,y(1)={y}_{c}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

- Use $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+B(0)+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- Use $y(1)=3$ with $A=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})+{y}_{p}(1) \\ 3 & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})+0 \\ B & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2n\pi x).

$$
\begin{aligned}6{z}^{2}+10z-1 & =0 \\ 6{z}^{2}+10z & =1 \\ 6({z}^{2}+\frac{5}{3}z) & =1 \\ 6[{z}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{5}{6}\cdot z+{(\frac{5}{6})}^{2}-{(\frac{5}{6})}^{2}] & =1 \\ 6[{(z+\frac{5}{6})}^{2}-{(\frac{5}{6})}^{2}] & =1 \\ 6[{(z+\frac{5}{6})}^{2}-\frac{25}{36}] & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{(z+\frac{5}{6})}^{2}-6\cdot \frac{25}{36} & =1 \\ 6{(z+\frac{5}{6})}^{2}-\frac{25}{6} & =1 \\ 6{(z+\frac{5}{6})}^{2} & =\frac{31}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{5}{6}$ and $q=\frac{31}{6}.$ Finally,

$$
p+q=\frac{5}{6}+\frac{31}{6}=\frac{36}{6}=6.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186265780 :question/id #uuid "e3fdc752-039f-5f05-8441-586cbafa095b" :question/math-academy-id "q-12983" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186184191 :knowledge-point/id #uuid :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "The equation $4{x}^{2}-6x-3=0$ can be written in the form $4(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p,$ and solve the equation." :question/worked-solution "First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-6x-3 & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2}-6x & =3 \\ 4[{x}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}x] & =3 \\ 4[{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{3}{4}x+{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}] & =3 \\ 4[{(x-\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{16}] & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x-\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-4\cdot \frac{9}{16} & =3 \\ 4{(x-\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4} & =3 \\ 4{(x-\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =3+\frac{9}{4} \\ 4{(x-\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{21}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-\frac{3}{4}.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x-\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{21}{4} \\ {(x-\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{21}{16} \\ \sqrt{{(x-\frac{3}{4})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{21}{16}} \\ |x-\frac{3}{4}| & =\sqrt{\frac{21}{16}} \\ x-\frac{3}{4} & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{21}{16}} \\ x-\frac{3}{4} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{21}}{4} \\ x & =\frac{3}{4}\pm \frac{\sqrt{21}}{4} \\ x & =\frac{3\pm \sqrt{21}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186399760 :question/id #uuid "eaa71aa3-e92b-5db0-96a6-7043b42bf47f" :question/math-academy-id "q-112524"} {:db/id 17592186506525 :question/id #uuid 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "The equation $-3{x}^{2}+36x-94=0$ can be written in the form $3(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q-p.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-3{x}^{2}+36x-94) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-36x+94 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-36x+94 & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-36x & =-94 \\ 3[{x}^{2}-12x] & =-94 \\ 3[{x}^{2}-2\cdot 6x+{6}^{2}-{6}^{2}] & =-94 \\ 3[{(x-6)}^{2}-36] & =-94\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{(x-6)}^{2}-3\cdot 36 & =-94 \\ 3{(x-6)}^{2}-108 & =-94 \\ 3{(x-6)}^{2} & =-94+108 \\ 3{(x-6)}^{2} & =14\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-6$, $q=14.$ Finally,

$$
q-p=14-(-6)=14+6=20.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186404343 :question/id #uuid "211d779e-92bf-5786-beb2-56b9bec0ebf9" :question/math-academy-id "q-86415"} {:db/id 17592186506548 :question/id #uuid :step/math-academy-id 26284 :step/next {:db/id 17592186185205}} {:db/id 17592186185028 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185352 :tutorial/content "We can use the method of completing the square to solve quadratic equations with leading coefficients. 

As an example, let's solve the following quadratic equation by completing the square:

$$
4x^2-8x+3 = 0
$$

First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-8x+3 & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2}-8x & =-3 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2x) & =-3 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2\cdot 1\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}) & =-3 \\ 4[(x-1)^{2}-1] & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, expanding the brackets, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4[(x-1)^{2}-1] & =-3 \\ 4(x-1)^{2}-4 & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we isolate the perfect square by adding  $4$ to both sides and then dividing by $4\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x-1)^{2}-4 & =-3 \\ 4(x-1)^{2}-4+4 & =-3+4 \\ 4(x-1)^{2} & =1 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \sqrt{(x-1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} \\ |x-1| & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x-1 & =\pm \frac{1}{2} \\ x & =1\pm \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =1-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2} \\ {x}_{2} & =1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=\dfrac12$ and $x=\dfrac32.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7d202804-803f-5139-b32a-fca689609abb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6214 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c9c761f1-c1eb-55db-b51b-2f4b7c894767" :step/math-academy-id 37719 :step/next {:db/id 17592186185029}} {:db/id 17592186185029 :step/content {:db/id 17592186184232 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186183914 :question/id #uuid "9815dede-5c47-5430-a58a-218313f78412" :question/math-academy-id "e-10014"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c872e855-895e-5369-8a79-cbdf21133548" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049250} {:db/id 17592186050044} {:db/id 17592186051078}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186184502} {:db/id 17592186184750} {:db/id 17592186272310} {:db/id 17592186272311} {:db/id 17592186272312} {:db/id 17592186272313} {:db/id 17592186388841} {:db/id 17592186506516} {:db/id 17592186506589}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Quadratic Equation Given a Corresponding Perfect Square"} :step/id #uuid "4923c949-f86d-5707-8ac7-0bcd1b408f05" :step/math-academy-id 37726 :step/next {:db/id 17592186184963}} {:db/id 17592186185205 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185300 :tutorial/content "Consider the quadratic equation

$$
ax^2+bx+c = 0,
$$

where $a\neq 0.$ We can derive a general solution to this equation by completing the square.

First, let's subtract $c$ from both sides to isolate the variable terms:

$$
ax^2+bx = -c
$$

Since $a\neq 0,$ dividing by $a$ gives

$$
x^2 + \dfrac{b}{a}x = -\dfrac{c}{a}.
$$

Next, we complete the square on the left-hand side and move the constant terms to the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{b}{2a}x=-\frac{c}{a} \\ {(x+\frac{b}{2a})}^{2}-{(\frac{b}{2a})}^{2} & =-\frac{c}{a} \\ {(x+\frac{b}{2a})}^{2}-\frac{{b}^{2}}{4{a}^{2}} & =-\frac{c}{a} \\ {(x+\frac{b}{2a})}^{2} & =\frac{{b}^{2}}{4{a}^{2}}-\frac{c}{a}\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the terms on the right-hand side over a common factor of $4a^2,$ we get

$$
\left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a}\right)^2  = \dfrac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}.
$$

Taking the square root of both sides yields

$$
x + \dfrac{b}{2a}  = \pm \sqrt{\dfrac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}}
$$

which can be simplified as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\frac{b}{2a} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we isolate $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{b}{2a}\pm \frac{\sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}\end{aligned}
$$

which simplifies as

$$
x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}.
$$

This formula is called the **quadratic formula**. You'll learn more about how to apply the quadratic formula in future lessons." :tutorial/id #uuid "cc56cc55-b423-5e0b-aed0-e07bdb86f874" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13276 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Quadratic Formula"} :step/id #uuid "3f1ff0dc-f8c4-5e2b-90b2-8f6efe37b016" :step/math-academy-id 461792}] :activity/title "Solving Quadratic Equations With Leading Coefficients by Completing the Square" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186184433} {:db/id 17592186185028 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185352 :tutorial/content "We can use the method of completing the square to solve quadratic equations with leading coefficients.

ax^2+bx = -c
$$

Since $a\neq 0,$ dividing by $a$ gives

$$
x^2 + \dfrac{b}{a}x = -\dfrac{c}{a}.
$$

Next, we complete the square on the left-hand side and move the constant terms to the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{b}{2a}x=-\frac{c}{a} \\ {(x+\frac{b}{2a})}^{2}-{(\frac{b}{2a})}^{2} & =-\frac{c}{a} \\ {(x+\frac{b}{2a})}^{2}-\frac{{b}^{2}}{4{a}^{2}} & =-\frac{c}{a} \\ {(x+\frac{b}{2a})}^{2} & =\frac{{b}^{2}}{4{a}^{2}}-\frac{c}{a}\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the terms on the right-hand side over a common factor of $4a^2,$ we get

$$
\left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a}\right)^2  = \dfrac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}.
$$

Taking the square root of both sides yields

$$
x + \dfrac{b}{2a}  = \pm \sqrt{\dfrac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}}
$$

which can be simplified as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\frac{b}{2a} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we isolate $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{b}{2a}\pm \frac{\sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}\end{aligned}
$$

which simplifies as

$$
x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}.
$$

This formula is called the **quadratic formula**. You'll learn more about how to apply the quadratic formula in future lessons." :tutorial/id #uuid "cc56cc55-b423-5e0b-aed0-e07bdb86f874" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13276 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Two Similar Polygons"}] :question/problem "Given that the two polygons shown below are similar, determine the similarity ratio.

*Hint: Consider the ratio of the **larger** polygon to the **smaller** polygon.*

![](images/f4/f4da94c11054e9e42b7dc9f6c085d3c6be5fdf026ba9d913fb7b060d56221967.png)" :question/worked-solution "Given two similar polygons, the similarity ratio is the ratio of any two corresponding sides.

Notice that, for example, $\overline{LM}$ is the longest side of $NLMP$. Hence, it corresponds to the longest side of $ABCD$, which is $\overline{BC}$.

Therefore, the similarity ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}
k &= \frac{BC}{LM} \\
&= \frac{33}{22} \\
&= \frac{3}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** The ratio of the smaller polygon to the larger polygon would be

$$
\dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)}=\dfrac{2}{3}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050481} {:db/id 17592186050563} {:db/id 17592186074215 :question/id #uuid "eb263d37-8e78-56ec-a2e2-6baa9048106c" :question/math-academy-id "q-53653"} {:db/id 17592186074216 :question/id #uuid "c21585d1-a9bd-5cd7-8318-9409c7971eef" :question/math-academy-id "q-53654"} {:db/id 17592186073913 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073599 :question/id #uuid "fd7f22e7-9aba-5936-beb1-56d3a5e016cc" :question/math-academy-id "e-2969"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "63b3448f-fe75-5152-a3c0-00b5129375c5" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050164} {:db/id 17592186050585} {:db/id 17592186051086}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074230 :question/id #uuid "989d7f36-2472-5b2c-8006-75c0dadde58a" :question/math-academy-id "q-53867"} {:db/id 17592186074231 :question/id #uuid "7fe89ce8-9227-5ed9-b379-a02e66f4b915" :question/math-academy-id "q-53919"}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Shapes Similar to a Given Polygon"} {:db/id 17592186073599 :question/id #uuid "fd7f22e7-9aba-5936-beb1-56d3a5e016cc" :question/math-academy-id "e-2969" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186073913 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "63b3448f-fe75-5152-a3c0-00b5129375c5" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Shapes Similar to a Given Polygon"}] :question/problem "Which of the following quadrilaterals are similar to $\mathcal{R}$ (other than $\mathcal R$ itself)?

![](images/5a/5a7c9208a16a639ef6b08855a6caaacb39c121dd4ccf45271d98fcc70f1a8fed.png)" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $\mathcal{R}$ is a rectangle, meaning all the angles measure $90^\circ$, and it has $2$ pairs of parallel congruent sides.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given polygons.

- $\mathcal{Q}$ is *not* similar to $\mathcal{R}$. The polygon $\mathcal{Q}$ is a rectangle, and the corresponding angles are congruent, but the ratios of the lengths of the corresponding sides are not the same:
$\dfrac{8}{6}\neq\dfrac{3}{3}$
- $\mathcal{P}$ is similar to $\mathcal{R}$. Indeed, $\mathcal{P}$ is a rectangle. Furthermore, the corresponding angles are congruent, and the ratios of the lengths of the corresponding sides are the same:
$\dfrac{4}{6}=\dfrac{2}{3}$
- $\mathcal{S}$ is *not* similar to $\mathcal{R}$ because $\mathcal{S}$ is not a rectangle (it's a parallelogram).

Therefore, the correct answer is "$\mathcal{P}$ only.""} {:db/id 17592186050164} {:db/id 17592186050585} {:db/id 17592186051086} {:db/id 17592186074230 :question/id #uuid "989d7f36-2472-5b2c-8006-75c0dadde58a" :question/math-academy-id "q-53867"} {:db/id 17592186074231 :question/id #uuid "7fe89ce8-9227-5ed9-b379-a02e66f4b915" :question/math-academy-id "q-53919"} {:db/id 17592186073914 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073600 :question/id #uuid "98596871-dc8e-5083-a773-1a70ffe1a159" :question/math-academy-id "e-2970"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "77da466d-77c4-5ea7-bedb-753601111c40" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049223}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074202 :question/id #uuid "7fef63c5-c407-51d5-9d32-4dca8baa115a" :question/math-academy-id "q-53543"} {:db/id 17592186074217 :question/id #uuid "54f2586d-fab4-5a22-aca5-63e15acba968" :question/math-academy-id "q-53665"}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining the Correct Similarity Statement Between Two Similar Polygons"} {:db/id 17592186073600 :question/id #uuid "98596871-dc8e-5083-a773-1a70ffe1a159" :question/math-academy-id "e-2970" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186073914 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "77da466d-77c4-5ea7-bedb-753601111c40" :knowledge-point/title "Determining the Correct Similarity Statement Between Two Similar Polygons"}] :question/problem "Given that the two quadrilaterals below are similar, write down a correct similarity statement.

![](images/bf/bfff4195302736df01985ca9db83d373243833023003730004cd93512467e4f4.png)" :question/worked-solution "First, let's find the measures of unknown angles. Since the sum of the measures of internal angles of a quadrilateral is $360^\circ$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
m∠A + m∠B + m∠C + m∠D &= 360^{∘} \\
55^{∘} + m∠B + 90^{∘} + 125^{∘} &= 360^{∘} \\
m∠B + 270^{∘} &= 360^{∘} \\
m∠B &= 90^{∘}
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}
m∠K + m∠L + m∠M + m∠N &= 360^{∘} \\
55^{∘} + 90^{∘} + m∠M + 125^{∘} &= 360^{∘} \\
m∠M + 270^{∘} &= 360^{∘} \\
m∠M &= 90^{∘}
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the quadrilaterals are similar, and

$$
∠A≅∠K, ∠D≅∠N, ∠C≅∠L≅∠B≅∠M
$$

So far, we have that

- $A$ corresponds to $K$, and
- $D$ corresponds to $N$.

From the angle measurements, it's unclear whether $C$ corresponds to $L$ or $M$ (these are all right angles). However, $C$ sits between a $125^\circ$ angle and a $90^\circ$ angle, and so does $M$ (whereas $L$ does not). So, we also have that

- $C$ corresponds to $M$, and
- $B$ corresponds to $L$.

Therefore, we conclude that a correct similarity statement is
$ABCD \sim KLMN$."} {:db/id 17592186049223} {:db/id 17592186074202 :question/id #uuid "7fef63c5-c407-51d5-9d32-4dca8baa115a" :question/math-academy-id "q-53543"} {:db/id 17592186074217 :question/id #uuid "54f2586d-fab4-5a22-aca5-63e15acba968" :question/math-academy-id "q-53665"} {:db/id 17592186073915 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073601 :question/id #uuid "8fda1604-bea3-5061-9a3f-a0ec86f95a41" :question/math-academy-id "e-2972"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "dca2a1be-4373-5572-9cf4-3c634079b1e9" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074218 :question/id #uuid "3e32b4ac-79f1-5405-9e5b-031cfee73d29" :question/math-academy-id "q-53668"} {:db/id 17592186074221 :question/id #uuid "5094de0a-acb0-55ab-93d8-6a76ba53eaf9" :question/math-academy-id "q-53776"}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Possible Lengths of Sides for a Polygon Given Dimensions of a Similar Polygon"} {:db/id 17592186073601 :question/id #uuid "8fda1604-bea3-5061-9a3f-a0ec86f95a41" :question/math-academy-id "e-2972" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186073915 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "dca2a1be-4373-5572-9cf4-3c634079b1e9" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Possible Lengths of Sides for a Polygon Given Dimensions of a Similar Polygon"}] :question/problem "Given that $ABCD \sim A'B'C'D'$, $AB = 3\,\mathrm{ft}$, and $BC = 4\,\mathrm{ft}$,
which of the following could be the values of $A'B'$ and $B'C'$?

1. ${A'B'} = 15\, \mathrm{ft}, \, {B'C'} = 20\, \mathrm{ft}$
2. ${A'B'} = 30\, \mathrm{ft}, \, {B'C'} = 44\, \mathrm{ft}$
3. ${A'B'} = 18\, \mathrm{ft}, \, {B'C'} = 24\, \mathrm{ft}$" :question/worked-solution "For similar polygons, the ratios of lengths of the corresponding sides should be the same.

- For option I, the ratios are the same:
$\frac{AB}{A^{′}B^{′}}|= \frac{3}{15} = \frac{1}{5}; \frac{BC}{B^{′}C^{′}}|= \frac{4}{20} = \frac{1}{5}$
So, option I indeed gives possible values of $A'B'$ and $B'C'$.
- For option II, the ratios are different:
$\frac{AB}{A^{′}B^{′}}|= \frac{3}{30} = \frac{1}{10}; \frac{BC}{B^{′}C^{′}}|= \frac{4}{44} = \frac{1}{11}$
So, option II does not give possible values of $A'B'$ and $B'C'$.
- For option III, the ratios are the same:
$\frac{AB}{A^{′}B^{′}}|= \frac{3}{18} = \frac{1}{6}; \frac{BC}{B^{′}C^{′}}|= \frac{4}{24} = \frac{1}{6}$
So, option III indeed gives possible values of $A'B'$ and $B'C'$.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186074218 :question/id #uuid "3e32b4ac-79f1-5405-9e5b-031cfee73d29" :question/math-academy-id "q-53668"} {:db/id 17592186074221 :step/content {:db/id 17592186075009 :tutorial/content "When writing a similarity statement, corresponding vertices should appear in the same position in the statement. For example, if we're given that

$$
ABC \sim PQR
$$

for two polygons $ABC$ and $PQR$, we can immediately deduce that

$$
\angle A \cong \angle P, \qquad \angle B \cong \angle Q, \qquad \angle C \cong \angle R
$$

We can also deduce that

$$
k = \dfrac{AB}{PQ}= \dfrac{BC}{QR} = \dfrac{AC}{PR}
$$

where $k$ is the similarity ratio." :tutorial/id #uuid "28869083-9c33-5d75-a178-1a1624e17f5e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4721 :tutorial/title "Correctly Writing Similarity Statements"} :step/id #uuid "0907e75c-35e4-5576-acda-f1ed2bced1b9" :step/math-academy-id 29154 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074921}} {:db/id 17592186074918 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074983 :tutorial/content "Two polygons are **similar** if they have the same shape (though they may have different sizes).

More precisely, two polygons are similar if the following conditions hold:

1. Their corresponding angles are congruent.
2. The ratios of the lengths of their corresponding sides are all equal.

To demonstrate, let's consider the triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle EFG$ below.

![](images/23/233fcb591a81d9ee6eef3caf1f4df0f0e959a18144177e89d5f0ac88c94525f4.png)

From the figure above, we see that the corresponding angles are congruent:

$$
\angle A \cong \angle E, \qquad \angle B \cong \angle F, \qquad \angle C \cong \angle G
$$

We also need to check whether the ratios of the corresponding sides are the same. That is, we have to check whether

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{AB}{EF} &= \frac{BC}{FG} = \frac{AC}{EG}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the lengths of the sides, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{AB}{EF} &= \frac{6}{12} = \frac{1}{2} \\
\frac{BC}{FG} &= \frac{4}{8} = \frac{1}{2} \\
\frac{AC}{EG} &= \frac{5}{10} = \frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

The ratios are the same. Therefore, we conclude that the triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle EFG$ are similar. The common ratio of the sides,

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

is called the **similarity ratio**.

To express mathematically that the triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle EFG$ are similar, we write

$$
\triangle ABC \sim \triangle EFG
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d16f60d4-ecf1-552e-82e5-d75e3cee2d89" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2312 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "64268339-5582-581d-80ef-13e6ca1ae5d8" :step/math-academy-id :step/content {:db/id 17592186074983 :tutorial/content "Two polygons are **similar** if they have the same shape (though they may have different sizes).

More precisely, two polygons are similar if the following conditions hold:

1. Their corresponding angles are congruent.
2. The ratios of the lengths of their corresponding sides are all equal.

To demonstrate, let's consider the triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle EFG$ below.

![](images/23/233fcb591a81d9ee6eef3caf1f4df0f0e959a18144177e89d5f0ac88c94525f4.png)

From the figure above, we see that the corresponding angles are congruent:

$$
\angle A \cong \angle E, \qquad \angle B \cong \angle F, \qquad \angle C \cong \angle G
$$

We also need to check whether the ratios of the corresponding sides are the same. That is, we have to check whether

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{AB}{EF} &= \frac{BC}{FG} = \frac{AC}{EG}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the lengths of the sides, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{AB}{EF} &= \frac{6}{12} = \frac{1}{2} \\
\frac{BC}{FG} &= \frac{4}{8} = \frac{1}{2} \\
\frac{AC}{EG} &= \frac{5}{10} = \frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

The ratios are the same. Therefore, we conclude that the triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle EFG$ are similar. The common ratio of the sides,

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

is called the **similarity ratio**.

To express mathematically that the triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle EFG$ are similar, we write

$$
\triangle ABC \sim \triangle EFG
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d16f60d4-ecf1-552e-82e5-d75e3cee2d89" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2312 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "64268339-5582-581d-80ef-13e6ca1ae5d8" :step/math-academy-id 9636 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074919}} {:db/id 17592186074717 :step/content {:db/id 17592186075009 :tutorial/content "When writing a similarity statement, corresponding vertices should appear in the same position in the statement. For example, if we're given that

$$
ABC \sim PQR
$$

for two polygons $ABC$ and $PQR$, we can immediately deduce that

$$
\angle A \cong \angle P, \qquad \angle B \cong \angle Q, \qquad \angle C \cong \angle R
$$

We can also deduce that

$$
k = \dfrac{AB}{PQ}= \dfrac{BC}{QR} = \dfrac{AC}{PR}
$$

where $k$ is the similarity ratio." :tutorial/id #uuid "28869083-9c33-5d75-a178-1a1624e17f5e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4721 :tutorial/title "Correctly Writing Similarity Statements"} :step/id #uuid "0907e75c-35e4-5576-acda-f1ed2bced1b9" :step/math-academy-id 29154 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074921}} {:db/id 17592186075009 :tutorial/content "When writing a similarity statement, corresponding vertices should appear in the same position in the statement. </tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=96,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.72.$

Now, since

$$
np=96(0.72)=69.12>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=96(1-0.72)=26.88>5,
$$

and $n=96$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.72,\frac{0.72(1-0.72)}{96}) \\  & ∼N(0.72,0.0021).\end{aligned}
$$

The probability we wish to find is
$P(0.7<\overset{^}{\,p}\le 0.8).$
So, we convert $\overset{^}{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.7<\overset{^}{\,p}<0.8) & =P(\frac{0.7-0.72}{\sqrt{0.0021}}<Z\le \frac{0.8-0.72}{\sqrt{0.0021}}) \\  & ≈P(-0.44<Z\le 1.75) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.75)-P(Z\le -0.44) \\  & =Φ(1.75)-Φ(-0.44)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.75) & =0.9599 \\ Φ(-0.44) & =0.3300.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.7<\overset{^}{\,p}<0.8) & =Φ(1.75)-Φ(-0.44) \\  & =0.9599-0.3300 \\  & =0.6299.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186512932 :question/id #uuid "ba83e244-060a-5dec-904e-55d3bc3fab0a" :question/math-academy-id "q-146974" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "05de7114-c6d2-5aa0-af39-01c4eb3c61be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-Φ(1.51)" :db/id 17592186512117} {:answer/id #uuid "71142195-0b10-524d-8d89-cc3312aea868" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-Φ(1.29)" :db/id 17592186512368} {:answer/id #uuid "8cfe4040-0a28-5e2a-beae-ec384a40584e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-Φ(1.78)" :db/id 17592186512429} {:answer/id #uuid "c1d038d4-8c45-51ea-a946-61383d3a330e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-Φ(1.93)" :db/id 17592186512562} {:answer/id #uuid "e08790cd-6ba8-55b1-8612-1e73f81cd371" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-Φ(1.34)" :db/id 17592186512640}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186512117} :answer-field/id #uuid "99799375-0cad-5fd7-aafe-9d47d5e34722" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186512805}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Suppose we take a random sample of size $n=88$ from a population where $44%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows:

![](images/2c/2c717541104571d6dce45dc88e30c4ff2dd42471d2348fe05b7d91ce395adae4.svg)

In other words,

$$
X_i \sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).
$$

Let's assume the sample size is less than (or equal to) $5\%$ of the population size. Under this condition, we've seen that $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n$ can be considered to be (approximately) independent and identically distributed, which means that

$$
X = \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p),
$$

where $B(n,p)$ denotes a binomial distribution, and

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p).
$$

Remember that $X$ represents the number of sample members with the characteristic.

Now, let's assume that $np > 5$ and $n(1-p) > 5$ so we can apply the normal approximation of the binomial distribution (i.e., the central limit theorem). Then,

$$
X  \approx N\big(np,np(1-p)\big).
$$

Furthermore, we've also seen that we can construct an estimator $\widehat{\,p}$ as

$$
\widehat{\,p} =  \dfrac{X}{n}
$$

where

$$
\textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p}] = p, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}] = \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

Since $X$ is approximately normally distributed, $\widehat{\,p}$ is also normally distributed. Therefore, the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ is given by 

$$
\widehat{\,p}\approx N\bigg(p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\bigg).
$$

Finally, since we usually don't know $p,$ we can use a particular estimate to approximate $\textrm{E}[{\widehat{\,p}}]$ and $\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}].$

**Watch out!** In this lesson, $N$ denotes the size of a population, while $N(\cdot,\cdot)$ denotes the normal distribution." :tutorial/id #uuid "d4cf166b-07f1-5e2e-9b9a-8147d42ce348" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9526 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "5ce0e2df-ecaa-5cb0-b322-b2b78e5030ce" :step/math-academy-id 187404 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189056}} {:db/id 17592186189056 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189501 :tutorial/content "Let's summarize everything we know about the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}\mathbin{:}$

- $np > 5,$ *and*

- $n(1-p) > 5$.

*Then, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as the normally distributed random variable 

$$
\widehat{\,p} \sim N\left( p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n} \right).
$$

*

"q-147386" :question/problem "A fitness center has $1600$ members, $480$ of which play tennis. If the center randomly samples $60$ members, find a normal approximation for the probability that more than $24$ members in the sample play tennis. You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ are given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

| $z$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.5\,$ | $\,0.9418\,$ | $\,0.9429\,$ | $\,0.9441\,$ |
| $\,1.6\,$ | $\,0.9525\,$ | $\,0.9535\,$ | $\,0.9545\,$ |
| $\,1.7\,$ | $\,0.9616\,$ | $\,0.9625\,$ | $\,0.9633\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=60,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=\frac{480}{1600}=0.3.$

Now, since

$$
np=60(0.3)=18>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=60(1-0.3)=42>5,
$$

and the $n=60$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.3,\frac{0.3(1-0.3)}{60}) \\  & ∼N(0.3,0.0035).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If more than $24$ members in the sample play tennis, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & >\frac{24}{60}=0.4\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the probability we wish to find is
$P(\overset{^}{\,p}>0.4).$
So, we convert $\overset{^}{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{^}{\,p}>0.4) & =P(Z>\frac{0.4-0.3}{\sqrt{0.0035}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>1.69) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 1.69) \\  & =1-Φ(1.69)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.69)=0.9545.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.4\le \overset{^}{\,p}) & =1-Φ(1.69) \\  & =0.0455.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "30aaec14-16cc-59bc-9876-aeee76db4409"} {:db/id 17592186513003 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188679 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5d1f49e2-0e08-5966-bf0b-33d79bc46bdb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-Φ(0.66)" :db/id 17592186512316} {:answer/id #uuid "873cc424-c085-5723-b881-20ef7fecbd77" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-Φ(0.52)" :db/id 17592186512413} {:answer/id #uuid "b6c0529c-fbdc-5cfe-88eb-01281ed4b7cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-Φ(0.58)" :db/id 17592186512534} {:answer/id #uuid "e538117d-c9dc-58a0-8c48-4a9c7a9e89b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-Φ(0.53)" :db/id 17592186512646} {:answer/id #uuid "ee346f5b-62c5-52d8-9668-4cfe0bea6f78" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-Φ(0.69)" :db/id 17592186512679}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186512534} :answer-field/id #uuid "9ab3a112-abbd-5b74-bf90-3997e193c1b2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186186354}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0faf39ad-2709-5ec7-94d0-99312772d48f" :question/math-academy-id "q-146155" :question/problem "A nationwide study found that $38%$ of families own a pet. $$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=88,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.44.$

Now, since

$$
np=88(0.44)=38.72>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=88(1-0.44)=49.28>5,
$$

and $n=88$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.44,\frac{0.44(1-0.44)}{88}) \\  & ∼N(0.44,0.0028).\end{aligned}
$$

$P(\overset{^}{\,p}>0.52).$
So, we convert $\overset{^}{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{^}{\,p}>0.52) & =P(Z>\frac{0.52-0.44}{\sqrt{0.0028}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>1.51) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 1.51) \\  & =1-Φ(1.51)\end{aligned}

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=96,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.72.$

Now, since

$$
np=96(0.72)=69.12>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=96(1-0.72)=26.88>5,
$$

and $n=96$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.72,\frac{0.72(1-0.72)}{96}) \\  & ∼N(0.72,0.0021).\end{aligned}
$$

The probability we wish to find is
$P(0.7<\overset{^}{\,p}\le 0.8).$
So, we convert $\overset{^}{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.7<\overset{^}{\,p}<0.8) & =P(\frac{0.7-0.72}{\sqrt{0.0021}}<Z\le \frac{0.8-0.72}{\sqrt{0.0021}}) \\  & ≈P(-0.44<Z\le 1.75) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.75)-P(Z\le -0.44) \\  & =Φ(1.75)-Φ(-0.44)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.75) & =0.9599 \\ Φ(-0.44) & =0.3300.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.7<\overset{^}{\,p}<0.8) & =Φ(1.75)-Φ(-0.44) \\  & =0.9599-0.3300 \\  & =0.6299.\end{aligned}

know how to factor a difference of squares, like $x^2-4$, but how do we factor an expression like $x^4-16$?

It turns out, we can use the exact same method!

First, let's rewrite the quartics as perfect squares:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{4} - 16 &= (x^{2})^{2} - (4)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, our expression resembles a difference of squares, which can be factored as follows:

$$
a^2 - b^2 = (a+b)(a-b)
$$

Using $a=x^2$ and $b=4$ in the above formula, we can factor our expression as follows:

$$
x^4 - 16 = (x^2 + 4) (x^2 -4)
$$

We can check that it is correct by doing the multiplication:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(x^{2} + 4)(x^{2} - 4) &= x^{4} - 4x^{2} + 4x^{2} - 4^{2} \\
&= x^{4} - 4^{2} \\
&= x^{4} - 16✓
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we can factor the expression further since it contains another difference of squares,

$$
x^2-4=(x)^2-(2)^2
$$

Factoring this difference of squares as well, we get the following final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{4} - 16 &= (x^{2} + 4)(x^{2} - 4) \\
&= (x^{2} + 4)(x + 2)(x - 2)
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1a6d86c2-9680-593d-8933-cd7477e24a45" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3276 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "aae3437b-917f-5a6d-937c-47cf9a1ab389" :step/math-academy-id ${f}_{\text{avg}}=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Applying the average value formula, we find that the average value of the function is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi -0}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{8}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate this integral using a substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Differentiating, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $-1$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{8}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{8}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-{\frac{1}{\pi }(\frac{{u}^{9}}{9})|}_{1}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9\pi }[(-1)^{9}-{1}^{9}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{9\pi }(-2) \\  & =\frac{2}{9\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186304792 :question/id #uuid "2e55b4cb-6c56-5cac-893d-482f84ce6bec" :question/math-academy-id "q-3289"} {:db/id 17592186304797 :question/id #uuid "ecd43ed3-12b1-5649-a96a-79cb243b0602" :question/math-academy-id "q-3295"} {:db/id 17592186304800 :question/id #uuid "24f38454-bd1c-55d7-83bd-a807c36fe3b4" :question/math-academy-id "q-3297"} {:db/id 17592186317521 :question/id #uuid "ca22e7ac-d65b-5ebd-9780-abfeab066eda" :question/math-academy-id "q-344648"} {:db/id 17592186317528 :question/id #uuid "ce1dc838-ac3c-58a3-9be3-5a30e3211516" :question/math-academy-id "q-344695" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186101022 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "55fab3ac-cad3-54bd-b07b-9159554b634c" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Average Value of a Function Over a Given Interval"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ed2abe4d-57c0-599d-b2da-3bc3a8e57a74" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2}{\pi }" :db/id 17592186316437}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "ed2abe4d-57c0-599d-b2da-3bc3a8e57a74" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2}{\pi }" :db/id 17592186316437} :answer-field/id #uuid "492b509c-6314-53ae-a2da-64e59ff1f2cb" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186316716}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Find the average value ${f}_{\text{avg}}$ of the function $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)$ on the interval $[0,\frac{\pi }{3}].$ Do not round the answer.

"![](images/df/dfa665cf99f35e5cd2edef04b3f334f0054bbce7fc9b66c519d59d30e77ba2a1.png)

The graph of the function $f(x),$ which is defined on $[0,10],$ is shown above. It consists of line segments.

Find the average value ${f}_{\text{avg}}$ of $f(x)$ on $[1,9].$ Do not round the answer.

${f}_{\text{avg}}=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The average value of a function on a given interval $[a,b]$ is 

$$
{f}_{\text{avg}}=\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the additive property of the definite integral, we write

$$
{\int }_{1}^{9}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{1}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{5}^{9}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{2}}.
$$

The 1st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [1,5].$ The corresponding region is a triangle, so we find the area using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot 2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have 

$$
{\int }_{1}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{1}=-4.
$$

The 2nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [5,9].$ The corresponding region is a triangle, so we find the area using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot 3 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
{\int }_{5}^{9}f(x)\,\text{d}x={A}_{2}=6.
$$

So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{9}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} \\  & =-4+6 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the formula for the average value, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9-1}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186317533 :question/id #uuid "6a9b3690-5bff-58f7-9210-58693a026b5b" :question/math-academy-id "q-344716"} {:db/id 17592186342169 :question/id #uuid ![](images/01/01597200b1f0e147fa8c53b6301d0c8e37208b5a6cce64cf0d9859d1220d8385.png)

 

Using the formula for the area of a trapezoid, we have that

$$
\eqalign{
\textrm{Area}\,(\textrm{R}) = \dfrac{1}{2}(3+7)(3-1)= 10.}
$$

For the rectangle to have the same area, we must have 

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =f(c)(3-1) \\ f(c) & =5 \\ 2c+1 & =5 \\ c & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can summarize what we've just done by saying that

$$
\int_1^3 (2x +1)\, \textrm d x= f(2) \cdot (3-1).
$$

This is an example of the **mean value theorem for integrals**, which states:

*If $f(x)$ is a continuous function on the closed interval $[a, b]$, then there exists a number $c$ in that interval such that*

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\, \textrm d x = f(c) \cdot (b-a).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c1b3241c-c8fd-514f-aa8c-a000710896d4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 986 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d75b1c61-1292-5625-8252-d8c10bae2e1b" :step/math-academy-id 618980 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101909}} {:db/id 17592186101909 :step/content {:db/id 17592186101021 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100733 :question/id #uuid "a0f21b4c-0f5c-5567-aaec-9da481d2e7ac" :question/math-academy-id "e-547"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "86221215-32a6-5c5a-bcd7-220e166bcee8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048187} {:db/id 17592186050819}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101335} {:db/id 17592186101336} {:db/id 17592186101382} {:db/id 17592186256385} {:db/id 17592186256391} {:db/id 17592186290568} {:db/id 17592186290569} {:db/id 17592186290572} {:db/id 17592186290575} {:db/id 17592186290580} {:db/id 17592186317508} {:db/id 17592186459215} {:db/id 17592186459232} {:db/id 17592186459242} {:db/id 17592186459273} {:db/id 17592186459274}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Points That Satisfy the Mean Value Theorem for Integrals"} :step/id #uuid "3e6aeea7-0134-5101-a19a-c37ab846bb82" :step/math-academy-id 618981 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101910}} {:db/id 17592186101910 :step/content {:db/id 17592186102035 :tutorial/content "The **average value** of a continuous function on a closed interval $[a,b]$ is given by

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:r=⟨-5,0,1⟩+t⟨-3,1,0⟩,\,Π:-3x+y-2z+27=0.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by writing the equation of the line as

$$
r=⟨-5-3t,t,1⟩.
$$

Let's also write the equation of the plane in the dot product form:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x+y-2z+27 & =0 \\ -3x+y-2z & =-27 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27 \\ r\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨-5-3t,t,1⟩$ into the equation of the plane, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27 \\ ⟨-5-3t,t,1⟩\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27 \\ -3(-5-3t)+1\cdot t-2\cdot 1 & =-27 \\ 15+9t+t-2 & =-27 \\ 10t & =-40 \\ t & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P,$ we substitute $t=-4$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨-5-3(-4),-4,1⟩ \\  & =⟨7,-4,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intersection point is $P(7,-4,1).$"} {:db/id 17592186244184 :question/id #uuid "7ed76edb-2aee-5101-83be-e4a973b64993" :question/math-academy-id "q-108891"} {:db/id 17592186304962 :question/id #uuid "8c9e4b1e-64e1-5274-81d9-5dc1e69f7cbb" :question/math-academy-id "q-33194"} {:db/id 17592186304967 :question/id #uuid "00b27684-fae1-56d0-a859-d1fc21cc59df" :question/math-academy-id "q-33197"} {:db/id 17592186304971 :question/id #uuid "c249fd8c-dcff-5201-89e1-bb6d2a206072" :question/math-academy-id "q-33201"} {:db/id 17592186314820 :question/id #uuid "5873c215-84fe-562e-9b4f-b99d76cb6e63" :question/math-academy-id "q-33968"} {:db/id 17592186342129 :question/id #uuid "156769fc-4325-56fe-a6f3-a488d1baa118" :question/math-academy-id "q-74004" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8e017315-e476-5fa0-8361-dc00652a6489" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2,0,1)" :db/id 17592186340405} {:answer/id #uuid "ad64653c-387b-56c4-988a-77711f82ccae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No intersection" :db/id 17592186340706} {:answer/id #uuid "af463bcf-e431-5d1e-a420-7660e1b98031" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-2,-5,4)" :db/id 17592186340726} {:answer/id #uuid "d8153fa3-e604-533d-b56e-b26114f3d4d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(3,1,5)" :db/id 17592186341045} {:answer/id #uuid "f86bd550-c5e7-5c4a-ad94-8436818324a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-5,4,2)" :db/id 17592186341326}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186341045} :answer-field/id #uuid "9343b686-98f1-53b8-a0c6-e7d798a3b52a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341638}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

l:r=⟨3,1,5⟩+w⟨-2,-5,4⟩,\,Π:r=⟨-5,4,2⟩+s⟨0,3,1⟩+t⟨2,0,1⟩.

$$

$$

Let's also write the equation of the plane in the dot product form:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2y+z-33 & =0 \\ x+2y+z & =33 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨1,2,1⟩ & =33 \\ r\cdot ⟨1,2,1⟩ & =33\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨-1+2t,-2+5t,6+4t⟩$ into the equation of the plane, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨1,2,1⟩ & =33 \\ ⟨-1+2t,-2+5t,6+4t⟩\cdot ⟨1,2,1⟩ & =33 \\ -1+2t+2(-2+5t)+6+4t & =33 \\ -1+2t-4+10t+6+4t & =33 \\ 16t & =32 \\ t & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P,$ we substitute $t=2$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨-1+2(2),-2+5(2),6+4(2)⟩ \\  & =⟨3,8,14⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intersection point is $P(3,8,14).$"} {:db/id 17592186402256 :question/id #uuid "cbfd2820-3a30-53a2-832d-407032fe3cf1" :question/math-academy-id "q-33987"} {:db/id 17592186442982 :question/id #uuid "2968eff5-6f3b-5cf4-97d0-686663582eb3" :question/math-academy-id "q-108369"} {:db/id 17592186475912 :question/id #uuid "07e33caa-9650-5834-8d9a-46cc82f723d1" :question/math-academy-id "q-108434" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "007d69dc-a2ca-580f-b0f7-74cbcfa1ebdd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No intersection" :db/id 17592186475444} {:answer/id #uuid "3a25e529-3954-5987-92eb-d533381cc44b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(25,31,-6)" :db/id 17592186475523} {:answer/id #uuid "52af092c-e727-5f18-8ff7-345347fe6d51" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-8,-13,5)" :db/id 17592186475562} {:answer/id #uuid "572842f6-cb5d-5a22-b2c9-50266f22eb6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(13,15,-2)" :db/id 17592186475570} {:answer/id #uuid "fca47535-789f-5b0b-98b2-271a04ca1b25" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-14,-21,7)" :db/id 17592186475823}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186475523} :answer-field/id #uuid "d8937436-576e-5320-a137-6b981c96167e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186475895}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$" :question/worked-solution "From the equation of a plane in the parametric form $r=p+tv+sw$, we have that its normal vector is $n=v\times w.$ In our case, the normal vectors to $Π$ is

$$

Therefore, the equation of the plane $Π$ in dot product form is

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨4,-3,-2⟩ & =⟨5,3,-4⟩\cdot ⟨4,-3,-2⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨4,-3,-2⟩ & =19.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨1,-1,2⟩+w⟨3,4,-1⟩$ into the equation of the plane in dot product form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨4,-3,-2⟩ & =19 \\ ⟨1+3w,-1+4w,2-w⟩\cdot ⟨4,-3,-2⟩ & =19 \\ 4(1+3w)-3(-1+4w)-2(2-w) & =19 \\ 4+12w+3-12w-4+2w & =19 \\ 2w & =16 \\ w & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $q$ of the intersection point $Q,$ we substitute $w=8$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}q & =⟨1+3(8),-1+4(8),2-8⟩ \\  & =⟨25,31,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨-2,-1,0⟩+t⟨3,2,4⟩ \\  & =⟨-2+3t,-1+2t,4t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Now, substituting $r=⟨-2+3t,-1+2t,4t⟩$ into the equation of the plane, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨3,-1,2⟩ & =25 \\ ⟨-2+3t,-1+2t,4t⟩\cdot ⟨3,-1,2⟩ & =25 \\ 3(-2+3t)-(-1+2t)+2(4t) & =25 \\ -6+9t+1-2t+8t & =25 \\ 15t & =30 \\ t & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P,$ we substitute $t=2$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨-2+3(2),-1+2(2),4(2)⟩ \\  & =⟨4,3,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get $P(4,3,8).$"} {:db/id 17592186119838 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119652 :question/id #uuid "f952e670-a673-5c15-913b-c396e8885142" :question/math-academy-id "e-4945"} $\Pi\mathbin{:}$

$$
l: \mathbf{r} = \langle 2,2,1 \rangle + t \langle 3,0,1 \rangle, \qquad \Pi:\mathbf{r} \cdot \langle 3,-5,1 \rangle = 7.
$$

How can we find the intersection point $P$ of $l$ and $\Pi?$

We start by writing the equation of the line in the form $\mathbf{r} = \langle 2+3t , 2, 1+t \rangle.$ Now, since $P$ must lie on the line $l,$ we can write its coordinates as $P(2+3t , 2, 1+t)$ for some particular value of $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$

![](images/d3/d3ba164eb98a53c463744e11d6593177ddde2a0a309f752e5d86b30db0d79925.png)

On the other hand, $P$ also lies on the plane $\Pi.$ So, the coordinates $P(2+3t , 2, 1+t)$ must satisfy the equation of the plane as well. Substituting the position vector $\mathbf{r} = \langle 2+3t , 2, 1+t \rangle$ into the equation of the plane and solving for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨3,-5,1⟩ & =7 \\ ⟨2+3t,2,1+t⟩\cdot ⟨3,-5,1⟩ & =7 \\ 3(2+3t)-5\cdot 2+(1+t) & =7 \\ 6+9t-10+1+t & =7 \\ 10t & =10 \\ t & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

To get the position vector $\mathbf{p}$ of the intersection point $P,$ we substitute $t=1$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨2+3(1),2,1+(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨5,2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intersection point is $P(5, 2, 2).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b2ca8cb0-0b92-5b99-ac8b-edd2f2a6dbb1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3259 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:r=⟨3,1,5⟩+w⟨-2,-5,4⟩,\,Π:r=⟨-5,4,2⟩+s⟨0,3,1⟩+t⟨2,0,1⟩.
$$" :question/worked-solution "From the equation of a plane in the parametric form $r=p+tv+sw$, we have that its normal vector is $n=v\times w.$ In our case, the normal vectors to $Π$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =v\times w \\  & =⟨0,3,1⟩\times ⟨2,0,1⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =3i+2j-6k \\  & =⟨3,2,-6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the plane $Π$ in dot product form is

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ & =⟨-5,4,2⟩\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ & =-19.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨3,1,5⟩+w⟨-2,-5,4⟩$ into the equation of the plane in dot product form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ & =-19 \\ ⟨3-2w,1-5w,5+4w⟩\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ & =-19 \\ 3(3-2w)+2(1-5w)-6(5+4w) & =-19 \\ 9-6w+2-10w-30-24w & =-19 \\ -40w & =0 \\ w & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $q$ of the intersection point $Q,$ we substitute $w=0$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}q & =⟨3-2(0),1-5(0),5+4(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨3,1,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection point is $Q(3,1,5).$"} :step/id #uuid "0227058d-e862-5e31-b5c8-bea4849a37b5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186484327}} {:db/id 17592186484313 :step/content {:db/id 17592186342127 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b2ccf68-fbc4-58ea-80f0-c47a1f4e61c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No intersection" :db/id 17592186339365} {:answer/id #uuid "1d364631-26c0-59a4-93c9-0842ba8027a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(19,10,16)" :db/id 17592186339381} {:answer/id #uuid "2bfe2f6a-4b05-5041-9be9-ec95d41ced84" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(18,8,12)" :db/id 17592186339510} {:answer/id #uuid "90fc5ea2-94e0-5824-91af-e274368bde07" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(18,11,16)" :db/id 17592186340429} {:answer/id #uuid "a5f82de1-4dec-5d15-9285-344580d1aa1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(8,-1,6)" :db/id 17592186340633}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186340429} :answer-field/id #uuid "3769c405-5ffb-59ea-8180-d6fbf6837b56" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341479}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8a17e320-306c-50fa-b84b-f8cbe958e629" :question/math-academy-id "q-73993" :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

Now, substituting $r=⟨1,-1,2⟩+w⟨3,4,-1⟩$ into the equation of the plane in dot product form, we get
