Then we have $X∼N(15,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find $P(X<12).$ But first, we need to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X>17)=0.1.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 17) & =1-P(X>17) \\  & =1-0.1 \\  & =0.9\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 17) & =0.9 \\ P(Z\le \frac{17-15}{\sigma }) & =0.9 \\ Φ(\frac{2}{\sigma }) & =0.9 \\ \frac{2}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.9)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.9)≈1.2816.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sigma } & =1.2816 \\ \frac{1}{\sigma } & =0.6408 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{1}{0.6408} \\  & ≈1.5605.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve for $P(X<12)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<12) & =P(X\le 12) \\  & =P(Z\le \frac{12-15}{1.5605}) \\  & ≈P(Z\le -1.92) \\  & =Φ(-1.92) \\  & =0.0274 \\  & ≈2.7%\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, approximately $2.7%$ of cookies contain less than $12$ grams of sugar."} :step/id #uuid "5bce04ca-70c6-54fe-8fc6-e22eeb0734f9" :step/next {:db/id 17592186507572}} {:db/id 17592186507572 :step/content {:db/id 17592186083975 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8cb42038-d4e2-5cd2-8193-28bac637ba07" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.13" :db/id 17592186082782} {:answer/id #uuid "292516a9-9b55-5825-97e9-ce95b5702014" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.87" :db/id 17592186082783} {:answer/id #uuid "3b79c1d9-f7d4-5316-be66-a07d9bb8fe63" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.92" :db/id 17592186082784} {:answer/id #uuid "698291c0-9ecf-5cf7-aa1b-9afe2e390f0d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.08" :db/id 17592186082785} {:answer/id #uuid "6aede979-f402-5d68-8ab7-96a5935c49a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.23" :db/id 17592186082786}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186082785} :answer-field/id #uuid "d097420f-f8f8-569f-a975-5e227fecbe9b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186082781}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "3e774eae-3ccc-5f1e-a35b-4ce8e1ddec45" :question/math-academy-id "q-94971" :question/problem "The test scores of a group of students are normally distributed with a mean of $73$ and a standard deviation of $5.$ What is the probability that a randomly selected student got a score of $80$ or more? $$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 80) & =P(Z\ge \frac{80-73}{5}) \\  & =P(Z\ge 1.4) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 1.4) \\  & =1-Φ(1.4)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Additionally, $3%$ of batteries last less than $1.75$ years. Find the mean $\mu $, rounded to $2$ decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $p$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.10\,$ | $\,0.15\,$ | $\,0.20\,$ | $\,0.25\,$ |

We know that $P(X<1.75)=0.03.$ Converting $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1.75) & =0.03 \\ P(Z\le \frac{1.75-\mu }{0.5}) & =0.03 \\ Φ(\frac{1.75-\mu }{0.5}) & =0.03 \\ \frac{1.75-\mu }{0.5} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.03).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.03)=-1.8808.
$$

Finally then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1.75-\mu }{0.5} & =-1.8808 \\ 1.75-\mu  & =-0.9404 \\ \mu  & ≈2.69.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c58cd6d2-7a47-5d68-ba83-ba5b2c86397f" :step/next {:db/id 17592186507584}} {:db/id 17592186507584 :step/content {:db/id 17592186507444 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d935e86d-2878-5713-88af-732c2cd4dd43" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9.05" :db/id 17592186507145}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186507145} :answer-field/id #uuid "eb3c213e-a427-5f30-8b6a-3f5985900ded" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186507383}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "62a29958-3d43-5575-a73a-6517a1734f8a" :question/math-academy-id "q-324461" :question/problem "The price of a deli sandwich is normally distributed with a mean of $\mu $ dollars and a standard deviation of $$1.10.$ In addition, in $90%$ of cases the price is between $$0.80\mu $ and $$1.20\mu .$ Find the average price, **rounding your answer to two decimal places**.

| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,0.6745\,$ | $\,0.8416\,$ | $\,1.0364\,$ | $\,1.2816\,$ | $\,1.6449\,$ | $\,1.8808\,$ | $\,2.3263\,$ |

We know that $P(0.80\mu <X<1.20\mu )=0.90.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.80\mu <X<1.20\mu ) & =0.90 \\ 2P(\mu <X<1.20\mu ) & =0.90 \\ P(\mu <X<1.20\mu ) & =0.45 \\ P(X<\mu )+P(\mu <X<1.20\mu ) & =0.5+0.45 \\ P(X<1.20\mu ) & =0.95.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1.20\mu ) & =0.95 \\ P(Z<\frac{0.20\mu }{1.10}) & =0.95 \\ Φ(\frac{0.20\mu }{1.10}) & =0.95 \\ \frac{0.20\mu }{1.10} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.95).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.95)=1.6449.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{0.20\mu }{1.10} & =1.6449 \\ 0.20\mu  & =1.809\,39 \\ \mu  & =\frac{1.809\,39}{0.20} \\  & ≈9.05\,\text{dollars}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "de38d27b-caa8-5826-b9f1-c99bfdbf34b2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186507592}} {:db/id 17592186507592 :step/content {:db/id 17592186507489 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ea413de4-f41d-5bd6-8d46-90d7116bd177" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "51.99" :db/id 17592186507195}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186507195} :answer-field/id #uuid "abe2d838-2efe-5d60-8dd7-942ce7ac6cc4" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186507349}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "bd63f548-8bbe-5de7-9356-fc14587f7fab" :question/math-academy-id "q-325117" :question/problem "The heights of oak trees in a park are normally distributed with a mean of $\mu $ feet and a standard deviation of $8$ feet. $$

$$

[{:db/id 17592186074538 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074992 :tutorial/content "Consider the right triangle below.

![](images/cd/cd056cb2c92d918412778089c0744525fb676a79047b0e779161c68db8210d54.png)

We know that

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\sin A = \frac{BC}{AC}, & \cos C = \frac{BC}{AC}, \\ \cos A = \frac{AB}{AC}, & \sin C = \frac{AB}{AC}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consequently,

$$
\sin A = \cos C
$$

and

$$
\cos A = \sin C
$$

Now, let

$$
m\angle A =\theta
$$

Then, since $\angle A$ and $\angle C$ are complementary, we have

$$
m\angle C = 90^\circ - \theta
$$

and we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin θ &= \cos (90^{∘} - θ) \\
\cos θ &= \sin (90^{∘} - θ)
\end{aligned}
$$

In other words,

- the sine of an angle equals the cosine of its complement, and
- the cosine of an angle equals the sine of its complement.

Sine and cosine are known as **cofunctions**. The latter is called **co**sine to indicate that it is the **co**function of sine." :tutorial/id #uuid "3b432c9c-d757-5975-9b24-999b2bce5a31" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2456 :tutorial/title far, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin θ &= \cos (90^{∘} - θ), \\
\cos θ &= \sin (90^{∘} - θ)
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the above properties, we can also derive cofunction properties for secant and cosecant. We start with

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sec θ &= \frac{1}{\cos θ} \\
&= (1)/(\sin (90^{∘} - θ)) \\
&= \csc (90^{∘} - θ)
\end{aligned}
$$

By the same reasoning, we can show that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\csc θ &= \sec (90^{∘} - θ)
\end{aligned}
$$

So we have deduced that secant and **co**secant are also cofunctions. To summarize:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sec θ &= \csc (90^{∘} - θ), \\
\csc θ &= \sec (90^{∘} - θ)
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by similar reasoning, it's possible to show that tangent and **co**tangent are cofunctions. Their cofunction relationships are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tan θ &= \cot (90^{∘} - θ), \\
\cot θ &= \tan (90^{∘} - θ)
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "04166248-ef12-5aa7-b46b-1a077920d60c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2562 :tutorial/title "Reciprocal Functions of Complementary Angles"} :step/id #uuid "60e93782-7e78-571a-affc-f9bf9070f1e5" :step/math-academy-id 11755 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074539}}] :activity/title "Trigonometric Functions of Complementary Angles" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186073937} {:db/id 17592186074538 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074992 :tutorial/content "Consider the right triangle below.

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186055525 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055999 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the integral of a power function multiplied by a constant, like $5x^2$. How do we proceed?

According to the **constant factor rule**, we can just take the constant factor out of the integral, like this:

$$
\int 5 x^2\, \textrm{d}x = 5\cdot \int x^2 \,\textrm{d}x
$$

Then, we solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
5 \cdot \intx^{2}dx &= 5 \cdot (\frac{x^{2 + 1}}{2 + 1}) + C \\
&= \frac{5}{3}x^{3} + C
\end{aligned}
$$

We can use this trick in general. Whenever the integrand is a function $f(x)$ multiplied by a constant $k$, we can simplify as

$$
\int k f(x)\, \textrm{d}x = k \int f(x) \,\textrm{d}x
$$

**Watch out!** We can only take *constant factors* out of integrals. We *cannot* take any variables out of integrals." :tutorial/id #uuid "f293df60-4b16-57ab-88c1-d784d4b5e36c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 698 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid 17592186074924}} {:db/id 17592186074923 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074984 :tutorial/content "Any transformation that maps a polygon to a similar polygon is called a **similarity transformation**.

Any combination of transformations made up of translation, rotation, reflection, and dilation will result in a similarity transformation.

To understand why this is true, remember:

- Rigid motions (rotation, reflection, and translation) do not change the lengths or angles of the original figure. They map polygons to congruent polygons. If two polygons are congruent, then they are similar.
- A dilation with scale factor $k$ multiplies all the lengths of the original shape by $k$ (leaving the angle measures unchanged), thereby producing a similar shape." :tutorial/id #uuid "622763c1-840b-5946-a1e7-feb59d8f0c89" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2315 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7ec1bc50-2134-5ed0-aa3d-e29348fd99e7" :step/math-academy-id 9647 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074720}} {:db/id 17592186074924 :step/content {:db/id 17592186073916 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073602 :question/id #uuid "54f05d2d-1137-5bc7-b56d-0215dc3895ad" :question/math-academy-id "e-2978"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d7545aba-d80b-58ab-9a56-25ad196da3ee" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074183} {:db/id 17592186074184}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Similarity Transformation Given a Polygon and Its Image"} :step/id #uuid "b8d1a4d2-47c1-5676-a5b1-d16b02e3ee67" :step/math-academy-id 9655 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074925}} {:db/id 17592186074925 :step/content {:db/id 17592186073917 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073603 :question/id #uuid "a75b57a8-4819-594a-9aa2-e35b54a68f6a" :question/math-academy-id "e-2993"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a8b5ef8e-6f13-5496-ae7f-c9fbaf3e25c7" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074207} {:db/id 17592186074209} {:db/id 17592186234140} {:db/id 17592186234141}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Similarity Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "3698100e-df7d-5666-8520-aa605b0f8eca" :step/math-academy-id 9670}] :activity/title "Similarity Transformations" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186073926} {:db/id 17592186074923 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074984 :tutorial/content "Any transformation that maps a polygon to a similar polygon is called a **similarity transformation**.

:knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements Given the Graph of a Derivative"}] :question/problem "The graph $y=g'(x)$, the derivative of $y=g(x)$, is shown below. Which of the following statements **must** be true?

1. $g(x)$ has a relative maximum at $x=1.5$
2. $g(x)$ has a relative minimum at $x=5$
3. $g(x)$ has an inflection point at $x=3.5$

![](images/58/582d792bf3854b0060e23e171fdc0c72e6486d09b0f1be47552ec4338d3f8ba1.png)" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $y=g'(x)$ intersects the $x$-axis at the points $A$ and $B$, as shown below.

![](images/fb/fbfcc5d729dea273d9b60c2ef80e10696aa0631698a7cb4ff009f54fb59b1ea3.png)

An extremum of $y=g(x)$ occurs when the graph $y=g'(x)$ changes its sign. Checking the first derivative at the points $A$ and $B$, we see that

- the point $A$, at $x=1.5$, is a relative maximum of $g(x)$ since the derivative $g'(x)$ switches from positive to negative, and
- the point $B$, at $x=5$, is a relative minimum of $g(x)$ since the derivative $g'(x)$ switches from negative to positive.

Therefore, statements I and II are true.

Now, an inflection point may occur where the second derivative $y=g''(x)$ is zero (the tangent line to $y=g'(x)$ is horizontal) or $y=g''(x)$ does not exist (a rapid change in the slope). Indeed, at the point $x=3.5$, which we label as $C$, we see that the slope of $g'(x)$ is zero, meaning that $g''(x)=0$.

![](images/e4/e4e945f8e45cd67982246dbd1798f3958eff114f7dc04ff98c3a30f5f570eff9.png)

We obtain an inflection point if the slope of the tangent line to $y=g'(x)$ changes its sign. Thus, we have an inflection point at $C$, where the slope goes from negative to positive. Therefore, statement III is true.

In conclusion, all three statements are true."} {:db/id 17592186176500 :question/id #uuid "3436a96c-5105-5b69-8c33-8e91f5bf63a8" :question/math-academy-id "q-49073"} {:db/id 17592186176501 :question/id #uuid "dfe41025-87a1-5739-a84f-52f72abada87" :question/math-academy-id "q-49094"} {:db/id 17592186175947 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175796 :question/id #uuid "7a25d851-2f79-5e70-bde2-eda99697fe3e" :question/math-academy-id "e-6851"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f73c50f7-fa8c-5d23-8699-e7e074f4251b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048188} {:db/id 17592186048420} {:db/id 17592186049604}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176512 :question/id #uuid "66da8c2e-9b52-5013-b42c-ca204234fc77" :question/math-academy-id "q-51408"} {:db/id 17592186176574 :question/id #uuid "2b96e246-6e1a-5cb7-9888-3f16ec267c72" :question/math-academy-id "q-80032"}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining Inflection Points and Intervals of Concavity Given the Graph of a Derivative"} {:db/id 17592186175796 :question/id #uuid "7a25d851-2f79-5e70-bde2-eda99697fe3e" :question/math-academy-id "e-6851" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186175947 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f73c50f7-fa8c-5d23-8699-e7e074f4251b" :knowledge-point/title "Determining Inflection Points and Intervals of Concavity Given the Graph of a Derivative"}] :question/problem "The graph of $y=f'(x)$, the derivative of $y=f(x)$, is defined on the interval $[-2,3]$ as shown below. Find all of the inflection points of $y=f(x)$ for $x\in(-2,3)$.

![](images/1d/1da07563588809f268054c88f684f47c701f4daeeb2bfdcb5c01d3f4d9aaa397.png)" :question/worked-solution "First, note that $f'(x)$ exists at every point on the interval $x\in [-2,3]$.

We need to investigate the behavior of $f''(x)$. We recall the following:

- When $f'(x)$ is increasing, we have $f''(x)>0$.
- When $f'(x)$ is decreasing, we have $f''(x)< 0$.

The function $f(x)$ has an inflection point at $x=a$, if the following two conditions are satisfied:

- $f''(x)=0$ or $f''(x)$ is undefined, and
- $f''(x)$ changes its sign (from negative to positive or vice versa) at that point.

We summarize the information from the given graph in the table below:

| $x$ | $(-2,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,3)$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $f'$ | $\searrow$ |  | $\searrow$ |  | $\nearrow$ |
| $f''$ | $-$ | $\text{not def.}$ | $-$ | $\text{not def.}$ | $+$ |

From the table, we see that $f''(x)$ changes its sign at the point $x=1$. Therefore, $x=1$ is a point of inflection of $y=f(x)$.

Note that the sign of $f''(x)$ does not change at $x=-1$, and so this is *not* a point of inflection."} {:db/id 17592186048188} {:db/id 17592186048420} {:db/id 17592186049604} {:db/id 17592186176512 :question/id #uuid "66da8c2e-9b52-5013-b42c-ca204234fc77" :question/math-academy-id "q-51408"} {:db/id 17592186176574 :question/id #uuid "2b96e246-6e1a-5cb7-9888-3f16ec267c72" :question/math-academy-id "q-80032" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186175947 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f73c50f7-fa8c-5d23-8699-e7e074f4251b" :knowledge-point/title "Determining Inflection Points and Intervals of Concavity Given the Graph of a Derivative"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ba01bfbb-971c-5482-9916-dfcab965dc07" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$x = ± 1$ and $x = ± 2$" :db/id 17592186175583} {:answer/id #uuid "deb335b0-e8cf-5685-ae78-8ce53b0a1221" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$x = ± 1$ and $x = 2$" :db/id 17592186175584} {:answer/id #uuid "014bcf6c-b9a5-5407-9a4c-6fc8f9628b44" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$x = 1$ only" :db/id 17592186175585} {:answer/id #uuid "034ecc8a-e7bd-5a63-91f5-54403ee1cee3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x = ± 1" :db/id 17592186175586} {:answer/id #uuid "4ae92f44-23f5-5100-92fb-7393a306fe5b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$x =-1$ only" :db/id 17592186175587}] :answer-field/id #uuid "b944462a-0d9c-56d1-ba28-a212c5ca0888" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186175582}] :question/problem "![](images/19/199a0809c86f57743fe954d1221656198f92339f146722928b46e598680d299f.png)

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186176603 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177063 :tutorial/content "Recall that we can use the second derivative to determine the concavity of a differentiable function $f(x)$:

- $f(x)$ is concave up on an interval $(a,b)$ if $f''(x) > 0$ on $(a,b)$, while
- $f(x)$ is concave down on an interval $(a,b)$ if $f''(x) < 0$ on $(a,b)$.

So, to determine intervals of concavity of $f(x)$ by looking at the graph of $f'(x)$, we need to pay attention to where $f'(x)$ is increasing or decreasing.

- If $f'(x)$ is increasing, then $f''(x)>0$, which means $f(x)$ is concave up.![](images/8a/8ac780a2dfa4d6c32449b750ff236568764de920d38e363d1badf4c7324c9c94.png)

- If $f'(x)$ is decreasing, then $f''(x)<0$, which means $f(x)$ is concave down.

![](images/2b/2bcc5e92916f582dc75450241c0223b55dab287d24e06b55e4d8fde56c7f927c.png)

Also, recall that $f(x)$ has an inflection point at $x=a$ if $f''(x)$ changes its sign around $x=a$. So, to determine the inflection points of $f(x)$ by looking at a graph of $f'(x)$, we need to pay attention to where $f'(x)$ switches from increasing to decreasing (or vice versa).

In other words, we need to pay attention to relative extrema on the graph of $f'(x)$.

17592186194453}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "For the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{3}y+x{y}^{3}+{y}^{2},
$$

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{\begin{bmatrix}∗ \\ y\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}0 & ∗ \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}∗ \\ y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the sum of the three missing expressions." :question/worked-solution "Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}, & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}y+{y}^{3} & {x}^{3}+3x{y}^{2}+2y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}6xy & 3{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} \\ 3{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} & 6xy+2\end{bmatrix} \\ {f}^{″}(1,0) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{\begin{bmatrix}x-1 \\ y\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-1 \\ y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
(x-1)+3+(x-1)=2x+1.

$$

Find the sum of the three missing expressions." :question/worked-solution "Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}, & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x & \operatorname{sin}⁡x-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x & \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y & -x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{bmatrix} \\ {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{\pi }{2}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{\begin{bmatrix}x-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ y\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{\pi }{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+(-\frac{\pi }{2})+(x-\frac{\pi }{2})=2x-\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281608 :question/id #uuid "2c3dba84-c7b2-5a37-bb07-b58c80773105" :question/math-academy-id "q-163142"} {:db/id 17592186281609 :question/id #uuid "f0b608b5-0740-5c5c-a8d8-286478d0cfd4" :question/math-academy-id "q-163143" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0889e045-221d-548d-8586-c263b14daf17" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2y-2" :db/id 17592186278673} {:answer/id #uuid "36bda793-84bc-523f-874b-ecf8461dfe2c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3y+7" :db/id 17592186279071} {:answer/id #uuid "b804339b-81d0-5458-8b89-1119bfccd852" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3y-3" :db/id 17592186280210} {:answer/id #uuid "bec80d1d-dc4a-5247-8229-4f3da550f0c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3y+10" :db/id 17592186280269} {:answer/id #uuid "ccd330d2-e165-5873-970a-d719dc56d528" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2y+8" :db/id 17592186280392}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279071} :answer-field/id #uuid "dd3902cd-4ea0-53f7-8e46-8bbcf944e194" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281220}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "For the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$

$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}, & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial:

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,1) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{x+y}+2x & \frac{1}{x+y}+3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix} \\ {f}^{′}(0,1) & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}+2 & -\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}} & -\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}+6y\end{bmatrix} \\ {f}^{″}(0,1) & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈1+\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y-1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{2}{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y-1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y-1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,2) & =e.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{3x-y} & -{e}^{3x-y}\end{bmatrix} \\ {f}^{′}(1,2) & =\begin{bmatrix}3e & -e\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to approximate the value of $f(2,2,2).$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =1+e, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}, & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈1+e+\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{2}{\begin{bmatrix}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,2,2) & ≈1+e+\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{2}{\begin{bmatrix}2-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =1+e+\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{2}{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =1+e+6+\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1 \\ 8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =7+e+\frac{1}{2}(14) \\  & =14+e.\end{aligned}

$$
f(x) \approx  \overbrace{f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)}^{\text{Linear approximation}} + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{2}f''(a)(x-a)^2}_{\textrm{Quadratic part}}.
$$

We can extend the concept of Taylor polynomials to multivariable functions. 

Given a twice-differentiable function $f(x,y),$ the **quadratic Taylor polynomial** of $f$ about the point $(a,b)$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(a,b)+{f}_{x}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)+{f}_{y}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)(y-b)+{f}_{yy}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In particular, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f(x,y)$ about the origin $O$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y \\  & \,\,+\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Later in the lesson, we will develop some intuition for why the quadratic part looks the way it does. However, increasing the number of variables significantly increases the number of terms in the Taylor polynomial. 

Ideally, we'd like a compact expression for the quadratic Taylor polynomial that works for all twice-differentiable functions $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R.$ This can be achieved using matrix notation. 

To see how, let's consider the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f(x,y)$ about $(a,b){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(a,b)+{f}_{x}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)+{f}_{y}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)(y-b)+{f}_{yy}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote ![](images/6f/6fe1832d2f4ae2b36446386e5d0ec7c41f898f4e575af9238695c37f7c427250.svg) and ![](images/49/496eacb98651e3fab4c0d0a7b44ab283fadad1c07243da485aeb0c4a059d5712.svg) then the total derivative of $f(x,y)=f(\mathbf{x})$ at $(a,b)=\mathbf{a}$ is given by

![](images/d6/d696700e295d9f43111ac53602b936a991b7766af654cedaa5afdae21b088a59.svg)

With that in mind, we can rewrite the linear part of the approximation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Linear approximation} & =f(a,b)+{f}_{x}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)+{f}_{y}(a,b)\cdot (y-b) \\  & =f(a)+[\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(a,b) & {f}_{y}(a,b)\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x-a \\ y-b\end{aligned}] \\  & =f(a)+[\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(a,b) & {f}_{y}(a,b)\end{aligned}]\cdot ([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]) \\  & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this is just our usual linear approximation of a function $f.$

The second derivative of $f$ at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a$ is given by

![](images/de/de2a75a6681e1e393b21b60de9d7aeee748a8e6d04010ab713b40f0f41f239cf.svg)

Therefore, using the fact that $f_{xy} = f_{yx},$ we can rewrite the quadratic part of the approximation using matrix multiplication as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Quadratic part} & =\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)(y-b)+{f}_{yy}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}x-a & y-b\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(a) & {f}_{xy}(a) \\ {f}_{yx}(a) & {f}_{yy}(a)\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x-a \\ y-b\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}([\begin{aligned}x & y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}a & b\end{aligned}])\cdot [\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(a) & {f}_{xy}(a) \\ {f}_{yx}(a) & {f}_{yy}(a)\end{aligned}]\cdot ([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our quadratic Taylor polynomial can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)}}+{{\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a)}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this formula is more compact and has clear similarity with the corresponding formula for functions with one variable:

$$
f(x) \approx  \overbrace{f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)}^{\text{Linear approximation}} + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{2}f''(a)(x-a)^2}_{\textrm{Quadratic part}}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "81df7b3f-d26d-54e0-baa0-de20a949b348" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7847 :tutorial/title "The Quadratic Taylor Polynomial in Matrix Form"} :step/id #uuid "3baad2a8-726c-5a26-b651-c058c266b286" :step/math-academy-id 45312 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199375}} {:db/id 17592186199375 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199503 :tutorial/content "The formula derived earlier works for multivariable functions with a finite number of variables.

$$

where the first derivative is

and the second derivative is

![](images/19/194e1d24c17ff07b1eb8e4036e13f30dee99cba17df11d5bada1a4d33d40b2a4.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "9075c096-fb26-52c7-ba1b-f03ecebd24e6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7848 :tutorial/title "General Formula For the Quadratic Taylor Polynomial in Matrix Form"} :step/id #uuid "3af1e2e0-59c9-5db1-ae9b-2ec6c9cd91fb" :step/math-academy-id 45313 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199376}} {:db/id 17592186199376 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198435 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198077 :question/id #uuid "1d13a6c0-0912-5089-81ed-c298bf747ccd" :question/math-academy-id "e-12563"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b91ae708-a63d-51ac-9ae0-f24724392858" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048859}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198637} {:db/id 17592186198643} {:db/id 17592186281602} {:db/id 17592186281603} {:db/id 17592186281607} {:db/id 17592186281608} {:db/id 17592186281609} {:db/id 17592186281610} {:db/id 17592186367811} {:db/id 17592186367825} {:db/id 17592186432372}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Quadratic Taylor Polynomial in Matrix Form"} :step/id #uuid "37ed5f21-d5e5-5cba-a75e-2083bfa15f8a" :step/math-academy-id 45314 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199378}} {:db/id 17592186199377 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199504 :tutorial/content "Here, we derive the formula for the second-degree Taylor polynomial of a multivariable function in vector form.

Suppose that the function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined by

![](images/df/dfa82e503eeaa38943edddc7d6982cf4893c73fd2f6d075dd390f51cd0450091.svg)

and is twice differentiable at $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{a}.$
By restricting $\mathbf x$ to a line through $\mathbf{a},$ we can consider $f$ as a function of one variable. Then, we'll use the second-degree Taylor polynomial of a single-variable function to derive the formula.

Let $\mathbf{x}_0$ be a constant vector in $\mathbb{R}^n.$ Then, the line through $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{x}_0$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{a} + t(\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{a}), \qquad t \in (-\infty, \infty),
$$

where $\mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{x}(1) = \mathbf{x}_0.$

Now, we define a function $F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by restricting the domain of $f$ to this line:

$$
F(t)
= f(\mathbf{x}(t))
%= f(\mathbf{a} + t(\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{a}))
$$

The second-degree Taylor polynomial of this single-variable function about $t=0$ is given by

$$
F(t) \approx F(0) + F'(0)t + \dfrac12F''(0)t^2.
$$

We can find the first derivative of $F$ using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a+t({x}_{0}-a)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot ({x}_{0}-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf{x}}$ is a row vector and $(\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{a})$ is a column vector, this is a scalar quantity and, hence, equal to its transpose:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot ({x}_{0}-a) \\  & ={(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot ({x}_{0}-a))}^{T} \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\end{aligned}
$$

With this, we can find the second derivative of $F{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}F}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})}^{T}) \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})}^{T} \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}f}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}({x}_{0}-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the first and second derivatives are given by

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t)={f}^{′}(x(t))({x}_{0}-a) \\ {F}^{″}(t)=({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(x(t))({x}_{0}-a).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the function and its derivatives at $t=0$ and using the fact that $\mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{a},$ we have

![](images/ba/ba4825ec7e9bb46e08df09c8b46b941c36a69ffd6e72081d09cd1ef6134a54d8.svg)

Putting these values into the second-degree Taylor polynomial of a single-variable function about $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & ≈F(0)+{F}^{′}(0)t+\frac{1}{2}{F}^{″}(0){t}^{2} \\  & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)({x}_{0}-a)t+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)({x}_{0}-a){t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using this polynomial to approximate the value of $F(1),$ and the fact that $F(1) = f(\mathbf{x}(1)) = f(\mathbf{x}_0),$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)({x}_{0}-a)\cdot 1+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)({x}_{0}-a)\cdot {1}^{2} \\ f({x}_{0}) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)({x}_{0}-a)+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)({x}_{0}-a).\end{aligned}
$$

However, $\mathbf{x}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is an arbitrary constant. Therefore, we can relax the assumption that $\mathbf{x}_0$ is fixed and replace it with a general point $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ near $\mathbf{a}$ to obtain the formula for the second-degree Taylor polynomial of a multivariable function in vector form:

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) \approx f(\mathbf{a}) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \dfrac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a}) (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "de526622-dda2-5168-9ec1-6b123e04fa54" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7862 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Quadratic Taylor Polynomial in Matrix Form"} :step/id #uuid "b64ce030-6e67-5cb0-926b-59488cada120" :step/math-academy-id 45339} {:db/id 17592186199378 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198436 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198078 :question/id #uuid "137d7caf-b232-5e21-9583-14d907a98624" :question/math-academy-id "e-12564"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b19cc766-bdc5-5ab2-aa4d-ebddf8311116" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198678} {:db/id 17592186198679} {:db/id 17592186284521} {:db/id 17592186284522} {:db/id 17592186284523} {:db/id 17592186284524} {:db/id 17592186284530} {:db/id 17592186284531} {:db/id 17592186367901} {:db/id 17592186367908} {:db/id 17592186432371} {:db/id 17592186432373}] :knowledge-point/title "Approximating a Multivariable Function at a Point Using a Quadratic Taylor Polynomial"} :step/id #uuid "ac6cf855-2b6f-5681-9ea0-41408d0715ca" :step/math-academy-id 45340 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199377}}] :activity/title "Second-Degree Taylor Polynomials of Multivariable Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186198498} {:db/id 17592186199372 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199501 :tutorial/content "Recall that the quadratic Taylor polynomial of a function $f(x)$ at the point $x=a$ is given by

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "81df7b3f-d26d-54e0-baa0-de20a949b348" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7847 :tutorial/title "The Quadratic Taylor Polynomial in Matrix Form"} :step/id #uuid "3baad2a8-726c-5a26-b651-c058c266b286" :step/math-academy-id 45312 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199375}} {:db/id 17592186199502 :tutorial/content "It's possible to derive Taylor polynomials for functions of more than two variables. However, increasing the number of variables significantly increases the number of terms in the Taylor polynomial. 

Ideally, we'd like a compact expression for the quadratic Taylor polynomial that works for all twice-differentiable functions $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R.$ This can be achieved using matrix notation. 

To see how, let's consider the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f(x,y)$ about $(a,b){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(a,b)+{f}_{x}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)+{f}_{y}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)(y-b)+{f}_{yy}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote ![](images/6f/6fe1832d2f4ae2b36446386e5d0ec7c41f898f4e575af9238695c37f7c427250.svg) and ![](images/49/496eacb98651e3fab4c0d0a7b44ab283fadad1c07243da485aeb0c4a059d5712.svg) then the total derivative of $f(x,y)=f(\mathbf{x})$ at $(a,b)=\mathbf{a}$ is given by

![](images/d6/d696700e295d9f43111ac53602b936a991b7766af654cedaa5afdae21b088a59.svg)

With that in mind, we can rewrite the linear part of the approximation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Linear approximation} & =f(a,b)+{f}_{x}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)+{f}_{y}(a,b)\cdot (y-b) \\  & =f(a)+[\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(a,b) & {f}_{y}(a,b)\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x-a \\ y-b\end{aligned}] \\  & =f(a)+[\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(a,b) & {f}_{y}(a,b)\end{aligned}]\cdot ([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]) \\  & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this is just our usual linear approximation of a function $f.$

The second derivative of $f$ at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a$ is given by

![](images/de/de2a75a6681e1e393b21b60de9d7aeee748a8e6d04010ab713b40f0f41f239cf.svg)

Therefore, using the fact that $f_{xy} = f_{yx},$ we can rewrite the quadratic part of the approximation using matrix multiplication as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Quadratic part} & =\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)(y-b)+{f}_{yy}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}x-a & y-b\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(a) & {f}_{xy}(a) \\ {f}_{yx}(a) & {f}_{yy}(a)\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x-a \\ y-b\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}([\begin{aligned}x & y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}a & b\end{aligned}])\cdot [\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(a) & {f}_{xy}(a) \\ {f}_{yx}(a) & {f}_{yy}(a)\end{aligned}]\cdot ([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our quadratic Taylor polynomial can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)}}+{{\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a)}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this formula is more compact and has clear similarity with the corresponding formula for functions with one variable:

$$
f(x) \approx  \overbrace{f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)}^{\text{Linear approximation}} + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{2}f''(a)(x-a)^2}_{\textrm{Quadratic part}}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "81df7b3f-d26d-54e0-baa0-de20a949b348" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7847 :tutorial/title "The Quadratic Taylor Polynomial in Matrix Form"} {:db/id 17592186199375 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199503 :tutorial/content "The formula derived earlier works for multivariable functions with a finite number of variables.

17592186199377 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199504 :tutorial/content "Here, we derive the formula for the second-degree Taylor polynomial of a multivariable function in vector form.

Suppose that the function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined by

![](images/df/dfa82e503eeaa38943edddc7d6982cf4893c73fd2f6d075dd390f51cd0450091.svg)

and is twice differentiable at $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{a}.$
By restricting $\mathbf x$ to a line through $\mathbf{a},$ we can consider $f$ as a function of one variable. Then, we'll use the second-degree Taylor polynomial of a single-variable function to derive the formula.

Let $\mathbf{x}_0$ be a constant vector in $\mathbb{R}^n.$ Then, the line through $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{x}_0$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{a} + t(\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{a}), \qquad t \in (-\infty, \infty),
$$

where $\mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{x}(1) = \mathbf{x}_0.$

Now, we define a function $F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by restricting the domain of $f$ to this line:

$$
F(t)
= f(\mathbf{x}(t))
%= f(\mathbf{a} + t(\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{a}))
$$

The second-degree Taylor polynomial of this single-variable function about $t=0$ is given by

$$
F(t) \approx F(0) + F'(0)t + \dfrac12F''(0)t^2.
$$

We can find the first derivative of $F$ using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a+t({x}_{0}-a)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot ({x}_{0}-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf{x}}$ is a row vector and $(\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{a})$ is a column vector, this is a scalar quantity and, hence, equal to its transpose:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot ({x}_{0}-a) \\  & ={(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot ({x}_{0}-a))}^{T} \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\end{aligned}
$$

With this, we can find the second derivative of $F{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}F}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})}^{T}) \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})}^{T} \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}f}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}({x}_{0}-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the first and second derivatives are given by

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t)={f}^{′}(x(t))({x}_{0}-a) \\ {F}^{″}(t)=({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(x(t))({x}_{0}-a).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the function and its derivatives at $t=0$ and using the fact that $\mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{a},$ we have

![](images/ba/ba4825ec7e9bb46e08df09c8b46b941c36a69ffd6e72081d09cd1ef6134a54d8.svg)

Putting these values into the second-degree Taylor polynomial of a single-variable function about $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & ≈F(0)+{F}^{′}(0)t+\frac{1}{2}{F}^{″}(0){t}^{2} \\  & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)({x}_{0}-a)t+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)({x}_{0}-a){t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using this polynomial to approximate the value of $F(1),$ and the fact that $F(1) = f(\mathbf{x}(1)) = f(\mathbf{x}_0),$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)({x}_{0}-a)\cdot 1+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)({x}_{0}-a)\cdot {1}^{2} \\ f({x}_{0}) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)({x}_{0}-a)+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)({x}_{0}-a).\end{aligned}
$$

However, $\mathbf{x}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is an arbitrary constant. Therefore, we can relax the assumption that $\mathbf{x}_0$ is fixed and replace it with a general point $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ near $\mathbf{a}$ to obtain the formula for the second-degree Taylor polynomial of a multivariable function in vector form:

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) \approx f(\mathbf{a}) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \dfrac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a}) (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "de526622-dda2-5168-9ec1-6b123e04fa54" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7862 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Quadratic Taylor Polynomial in Matrix Form"} :step/id #uuid "b64ce030-6e67-5cb0-926b-59488cada120" :step/math-academy-id 45339} {:db/id 17592186199504 :tutorial/content "Here, we derive the formula for the second-degree Taylor polynomial of a multivariable function in vector form.

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ is given by

Find the sum of the six missing expressions." :question/worked-solution "Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defened by 

$$

$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}}_{x=a}

Find the sum of the three missing expressions." :question/worked-solution "Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}, & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x & \operatorname{sin}⁡x-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x & \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y & -x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{bmatrix} \\ {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{\pi }{2}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{\begin{bmatrix}x-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ y\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{\pi }{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+(-\frac{\pi }{2})+(x-\frac{\pi }{2})=2x-\frac{3\pi }{2}.

[{:db/id 17592186084102 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084442 :tutorial/content "Suppose we roll a fair die. Then, the sample space $\mathcal S$ of this experiment is

$$
\mathcal{S} = \{1,2,3,4,5,6\}
$$

Now, let's consider the event
$X = \{6\}$.
This means that $X$ is the event "the die lands on $6$." We know that

$$
P(X) = \dfrac{1}{6}
$$

because there are $6$ equally likely outcomes and only $1$ of those outcomes is a $6$.

We can represent the entire sample space $\mathcal S$, the event $X$, and its probability using a **Venn diagram**.

![](images/96/966be6be009751b755fbcaca9f037e0c4ee281525a94e50a9a19631dc7cd4e1f.png)

Note the following important points:

- The area inside the rectangle represents the sample space $\mathcal S$.
- The area inside the circle (shaded blue) represents the event $X$.
- The number inside the blue circle represents the probability of $X$.
- The area inside the rectangle but outside the circle represents the event $X'$, the complement of $X$. In our case, the complement is
$X' = \{1,2,3,4,5\}$,
which consists of every event other than throwing a $6$.

For any event $X$, we have

$$
P(X) +P\left(X'\right) = 1
$$

Note that the above formula can be rearranged into either of the following equivalent forms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X) &= 1 - P(X^{′}) \\
P(X^{′}) &= 1 - P(X)
\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we can calculate

$$
P\left(X'\right)
$$

as

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X^{′}) &= 1 - P(X) \\
&= 1 - \frac{1}{6} \\
&= \frac{5}{6}
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the sample space $\mathcal S$ contains every possible event, we sometimes write

$$
P(\mathcal S) = 1
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "af5371a2-dcfe-5de0-b0ab-f82c96a0b759" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3657 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "93f32069-023f-5d69-983e-2273e36c3952" :step/math-academy-id {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186083470} {:db/id 17592186084102 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084442 :tutorial/content "Suppose we roll a fair die. Then, the sample space $\mathcal S$ of this experiment is

$$
\mathcal{S} = \{1,2,3,4,5,6\}
$$

Now, let's consider the event
$X = \{6\}$.
This means that $X$ is the event "the die lands on $6$." We know that

$$
P(X) = \dfrac{1}{6}
$$

because there are $6$ equally likely outcomes and only $1$ of those outcomes is a $6$.

We can represent the entire sample space $\mathcal S$, the event $X$, and its probability using a **Venn diagram**.

![](images/96/966be6be009751b755fbcaca9f037e0c4ee281525a94e50a9a19631dc7cd4e1f.png)

Note the following important points:

- The area inside the rectangle represents the sample space $\mathcal S$.
- The area inside the circle (shaded blue) represents the event $X$.
- The number inside the blue circle represents the probability of $X$.
- The area inside the rectangle but outside the circle represents the event $X'$, the complement of $X$. In our case, the complement is
$X' = \{1,2,3,4,5\}$,
which consists of every event other than throwing a $6$.

For any event $X$, we have

$$
P(X) +P\left(X'\right) = 1
$$

Note that the above formula can be rearranged into either of the following equivalent forms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X) &= 1 - P(X^{′}) \\
P(X^{′}) &= 1 - P(X)
\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we can calculate

$$
P\left(X'\right)
$$

as

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X^{′}) &= 1 - P(X) \\
&= 1 - \frac{1}{6} \\
&= \frac{5}{6}
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the sample space $\mathcal S$ contains every possible event, we sometimes write

$$
P(\mathcal S) = 1
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "af5371a2-dcfe-5de0-b0ab-f82c96a0b759" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3657 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "93f32069-023f-5d69-983e-2273e36c3952" :step/math-academy-id 20492 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084132}} {:db/id 17592186084442 :tutorial/content "Suppose we roll a fair die. $x.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $a$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $b$ equals the zero vector only when the vectors are perpendicular. 

So, we must have

$$
a⊥b\,⟹\,a\cdot b=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & ={a}_{x}\cdot {b}_{x}+{a}_{y}\cdot {b}_{y}+{a}_{z}\cdot {b}_{z} \\  & =2\cdot x+(-1)\cdot (-4)+(-2)\cdot 0 \\  & =2x+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =0 \\ 2x+4 & =0 \\ 2x & =-4 \\ x & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186290297 :question/id #uuid "6c452b5c-8f3c-5759-a6a2-00c200b73978" :question/math-academy-id "q-212462"} {:db/id 17592186292822 :question/id #uuid 1295} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186106562 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107166 :tutorial/content "The **vector projection** of a vector $\mathbf{a}$ onto another vector $\mathbf{b}$ is the portion that the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends along $\mathbf{b}.$

For example, consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ shown below. Suppose we know that $|\mathbf{a}|=2,$ $|\mathbf{b}|=3,$ and the angle between the vectors is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

![](images/a2/a28278cf12885ab7f845407ac2fa7f4ffa00dbe30849a3f8ff41f02e134ed3a0.png)

The starting point of the vector projection is $O,$ and the ending point will be the point $P$ that lies on the line containing $\mathbf{b}$ with $AP \perp \mathbf{b},$ as shown below.

![](images/f0/f0b267fb009e79eb16f86be42edc2c835808b28aa3eaf1c7e857300224ee01ec.png)

The vector $\overrightarrow{OP}$ is called the **vector projection** of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}.$ It is denoted as $\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a},$ and it is computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =OP\cdot u \\  & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u\end{aligned}
$$

where $\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} = |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta$ is the scalar projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{u}$ is a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{b}.$

First, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5962a19e-bb12-54d8-b53a-24578711fa53" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9051 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "26031206-512a-5b41-90d5-299987889655" :step/math-academy-id 121755 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106650}} {:db/id 17592186106563 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105701 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105478 :question/id #uuid "3278333b-a29e-54c5-bc94-b5525bc6f751" :question/math-academy-id "e-14617"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7c9317eb-d1ce-5f42-b69b-a37e643b865b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049360} {:db/id 17592186049653}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106111} {:db/id 17592186106480} {:db/id 17592186287856} {:db/id 17592186287939} {:db/id 17592186292817} {:db/id 17592186292818} {:db/id 17592186297479} {:db/id 17592186297480} {:db/id 17592186339000} {:db/id 17592186339001} {:db/id 17592186339002} {:db/id 17592186441580} {:db/id 17592186441582} {:db/id 17592186441585} {:db/id 17592186441586} {:db/id 17592186480688}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Vector Projection Using Angle and Magnitude"} :step/id #uuid "e6fd410f-37e5-5a4e-a29d-c160c7d2a397" :step/math-academy-id 121756 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106564}} {:db/id 17592186106564 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107167 :tutorial/content "We have been using the following formula for the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} =\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{u}
$$

However, we can write an alternative formula using the formula for the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the original formula for the vector projection, and also substituting $\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{| \, \mathbf{b} \, |},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}\cdot \frac{b}{|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,{|}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, another general formula for the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e4098700-6d5c-5618-90a8-8dea2d4dbed0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9052 :tutorial/title "A General Formula"} :step/id #uuid "a78e2420-8af1-50c7-9a19-b4ceac9bcde4" "146819e4-ecad-5e47-8884-a05b59624d07" :step/math-academy-id 121763} {:db/id 17592186106567 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107168 :tutorial/content "Notice that if two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are perpendicular, then by projecting $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ (or $\mathbf{b}$ onto $\mathbf{a}$), we obtain the zero vector.

For example, the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto a perpendicular vector $\mathbf{b}$ looks as follows:

![](images/91/9163eda36b752f1e36195b8b5a1d40bf545ec21a3988f5480d6ddcbb926c00ea.png)

Furthermore, we have the following fact:

*If $\mathbf{a}$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $\mathbf{b}$ equals the zero vector if and only if the vectors are perpendicular.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "97117437-4034-5cb8-84a6-675d75d4f874" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9059 :tutorial/title "Projecting Perpendicular Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "ec38d18e-577a-5ebc-8349-60991ef75b80" :step/math-academy-id 121766 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106566}} {:db/id 17592186106650 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107181 :tutorial/content "When finding the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b},$ we sometimes find that the resulting projection vector points in the opposite direction to $\mathbf{b}.$ This happens when the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends in the direction opposite to that of $\mathbf{b}.$

![](images/0e/0e973e6f6484a9aad863ebfe89fc1ea6356d6a50844931306c6aa2b63be18a8a.png)

Consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ where it is known that 

$$
|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2,\qquad |\,\mathbf{b}\,|=3,\qquad \theta = 135^\circ.
$$

Let's calculate $\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}.$ 

First, notice that the angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ is obtuse. This means we expect the projection vector to point in the opposite direction to that of $\mathbf b.$

Next, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡({135}^{∘}) \\  & =2\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the scalar projection is negative. 

Then, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$

This vector points in the direction opposite to $\mathbf{b},$ as expected." :tutorial/id #uuid "2df5fde5-316c-5962-8f0d-56362287c447" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9677 :tutorial/title "The Direction of the Projection Vector"} :step/id #uuid "fdc39c18-bf51-5a32-a828-404d1e341f7a" :step/math-academy-id 187844 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106563}}] :activity/title "Calculating a Vector Projection" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186105967} {:db/id 17592186106562 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107166 :tutorial/content "The **vector projection** of a vector $\mathbf{a}$ onto another vector $\mathbf{b}$ is the portion that the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends along $\mathbf{b}.$

The starting point of the vector projection is $O,$ and the ending point will be the point $P$ that lies on the line containing $\mathbf{b}$ with $AP \perp \mathbf{b},$ as shown below.

![](images/f0/f0b267fb009e79eb16f86be42edc2c835808b28aa3eaf1c7e857300224ee01ec.png)

The vector $\overrightarrow{OP}$ is called the **vector projection** of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}.$ It is denoted as $\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a},$ and it is computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =OP\cdot u \\  & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u\end{aligned}
$$

where $\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} = |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta$ is the scalar projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{u}$ is a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{b}.$

First, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5962a19e-bb12-54d8-b53a-24578711fa53" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9051 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186106650 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107181 :tutorial/content "When finding the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b},$ we sometimes find that the resulting projection vector points in the opposite direction to $\mathbf{b}.$ This happens when the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends in the direction opposite to that of $\mathbf{b}.$

![](images/0e/0e973e6f6484a9aad863ebfe89fc1ea6356d6a50844931306c6aa2b63be18a8a.png)

Consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ where it is known that 

$$
|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2,\qquad |\,\mathbf{b}\,|=3,\qquad \theta = 135^\circ.
$$

Let's calculate $\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}.$ 

First, notice that the angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ is obtuse. This means we expect the projection vector to point in the opposite direction to that of $\mathbf b.$

Next, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡({135}^{∘}) \\  & =2\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the scalar projection is negative. 

Then, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$

This vector points in the direction opposite to $\mathbf{b},$ as expected." :tutorial/id #uuid "2df5fde5-316c-5962-8f0d-56362287c447" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9677 :tutorial/title "The Direction of the Projection Vector"} :step/id #uuid "fdc39c18-bf51-5a32-a828-404d1e341f7a" :step/math-academy-id 187844 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106563}} {:db/id 17592186106563 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105701 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105478 :question/id #uuid "3278333b-a29e-54c5-bc94-b5525bc6f751" :question/math-academy-id "e-14617"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7c9317eb-d1ce-5f42-b69b-a37e643b865b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049360} {:db/id 17592186049653}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106111} {:db/id 17592186106480} {:db/id 17592186287856} {:db/id 17592186287939} {:db/id 17592186292817} {:db/id 17592186292818} {:db/id 17592186297479} {:db/id 17592186297480} {:db/id 17592186339000} {:db/id 17592186339001} {:db/id 17592186339002} {:db/id 17592186441580} {:db/id 17592186441582} {:db/id 17592186441585} {:db/id 17592186441586} {:db/id 17592186480688}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Vector Projection Using Angle and Magnitude"} :step/id #uuid "e6fd410f-37e5-5a4e-a29d-c160c7d2a397" :step/math-academy-id 121756 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106564}} {:db/id 17592186106564 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107167 :tutorial/content "We have been using the following formula for the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} =\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{u}
$$

However, we can write an alternative formula using the formula for the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the original formula for the vector projection, and also substituting $\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{| \, \mathbf{b} \, |},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}\cdot \frac{b}{|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,{|}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b.\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Since $a$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $b$ equals the zero vector only when the vectors are perpendicular.

So, we must have

$$
a⊥b\,⟹\,a\cdot b=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & ={a}_{x}\cdot {b}_{x}+{a}_{y}\cdot {b}_{y}+{a}_{z}\cdot {b}_{z} \\  & =t\cdot 4+(-4)\cdot 1+1\cdot 0 \\  & =4t-4+0 \\  & =4t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =0 \\ 4t-4 & =0 \\ 4t & =4 \\ t & =1 \\ t & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "333ded1a-53b9-5952-8d65-b4f24b2126f6"} {:db/id 17592186487424 :step/content {:db/id 17592186290296 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "085237b3-7339-507a-81da-41e8838a4e5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186288096} {:answer/id #uuid "2547952c-6d6d-51dd-84d9-5d6dddcecc24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186288278} {:answer/id #uuid "348d85f2-eb5b-5146-8401-4763298c0ead" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186288381} {:answer/id #uuid "81de0d68-8b33-5042-b528-9c369770b979" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186288908} {:answer/id #uuid "983ed9cb-19d2-5826-8970-1323081a65d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186289052}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186289052} :answer-field/id #uuid "5656f1d3-8dfe-58cd-9391-206ef0a86ac4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186289911}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "cbcf41af-6f81-5a46-9b85-441a34ac9cb2" :question/math-academy-id "q-212459" :question/problem "Let $a=⟨2,-1,-2⟩$ and $b=⟨x,-4,0⟩.$ Given that the projection of $a$ onto $b$ is the zero vector, find the value of $x.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $a$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $b$ equals the zero vector only when the vectors are perpendicular.

$$"} :step/id #uuid "acc822ee-4c60-569f-b9f3-f99814a03662" :step/next {:db/id 17592186487424}} {:db/id 17592186487441 :step/content {:db/id 17592186299659 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f1e74cda-962f-530c-9dc5-da6fa3027618" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186298576}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186298576} :answer-field/id #uuid "3ebbdb00-7250-5b52-a3d7-5e3a06732032" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186298855} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7c9bd58c-c3aa-5aac-8af2-0f2dd4d21cd2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186298091}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186298091} :answer-field/id #uuid "4ca49e40-42ef-549f-8cba-a8415f643eee" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186298892} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26a218fd-1c69-51ca-837a-ec2ac174e881" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186297712}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186297712} :answer-field/id #uuid "9a211abc-329d-5e8e-a21a-d845d97c0b27" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186299145}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "47bb7ff9-8595-5c3c-8469-6716c5ae622e" :question/math-academy-id "q-317924" :question/problem "Let $u=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $v=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ Find the vector projection of $u$ onto $v.$

$⟩$" :question/worked-solution "Using the formula for the vector projection, we obtain

"Consider the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}+3y=f(x),\,y(0)=-1
$$

where $f(x)$ is a $2$-periodic function. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(0)=0.$*

The solution is 

$y(x)∼$  
{{field-1}} 
$+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=f(x)$ is given by

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},
$$

where ${y}_{c}$ is the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we find the homogeneous solution. The general solution of ${y}^{′}+3y=0$ is 

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-3x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

Next, we identify the form of the general solution. Because the operator ${y}^{′}+3y$ involves a first derivative, a periodic forcing function $f(x)$ results in a particular solution containing both sine and cosine terms:

$$
y(x)∼A{e}^{-3x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))
$$

Now, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=-1.$ Using the hint that the particular solution part evaluates to zero at $x=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A{e}^{-3(0)}+{y}_{p}(0) \\ -1 & =A(1)+0 \\ A & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $A$ back into the homogeneous part:

$$
{y}_{c}=-{e}^{-3x}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼-{e}^{-3x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365936 :question/id #uuid "0bafe4c7-5c26-53ec-8fd3-af5a2bac498d" :question/math-academy-id "q-343732" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "91505a79-2ea5-54d7-95d8-90e5cea46420" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{e}^{4x}" :db/id 17592186365938} {:answer/id #uuid "e6e484f7-c12f-51da-8084-5c596183b805" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5e^{4x}" :db/id 17592186507911}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186507911} :answer-field/id #uuid "fa3102c8-b53d-52e0-8f47-cacae0ffde3c" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365937}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the initial value problem
